Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 110, to amend the Dominion Elections Act. He said: This is one of the Bills which was reported by the select special Committee appointed to consider the advisability of amending the Dominion Elections Act and the Dominion Controverted Elections Act. In this Bill, they propose first to repeal certain provisions in force in Saskatchewan and Alberta which permit a voter presenting himself at the polls after the lists have been completed to vote by simply swearing as to his qualifications. The same provision holds good in the Yukon, and it is not proposed to alter it as regards that territory. In the view of the committee, the conditions which justify it have ceased to exist in the two provinces mentioned. The next provision of the Bill is to make an amendment with regard to deferred elections. The change effected by "the Redistribution Act in certain constituencies altered the names of those constituencies as they appear in the present Act, making the provision to defer the election no longer applicable. The Bill does not purpose to provide for deferred elections in the entire portion of the constituencies that have been composed of parts of those constituencies in which they were previously permissible, but only in these new constituencies where conditions require it. There is also an amendment to make provision with regard to cases where a candidate may die after nomination, to assimilate the condition prevailing in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan to that prevailing in the rest of the country. There is a provision to prolong the hours of polling from eight to six instead of from nine to five, and a provision requiring employers to give an extra hour over and above the noon hour to their employees to 
enable them to vote, without making any deduction in their pay. There is also a provision - for correcting an error in the French version of one of the sections of the Act as it now stands. Furthermore, the schedule containing the nomination paper is proposed to be amended so as to require the candidate nominated to insert in the * nomination paper an address at which all processes or papers with regard to the election, or any contestation of the election, may be served upon him.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 109, to amend the Dominion Controverted Elections Act. He said: Dealing with the provisions which this Bill proposes to make as a whole, I may say their purpose is to simplify the procedure in controverted elections and to expedite the trial. There are provisions with regard to the proof of qualification of the petitioner, which make the production of the list upon which a man figures as an elector in the district conclusive proof of his qualification. The forms of the petition and the counter petition are modified so as to make them more simple, while at the same time giving more specific information to the party against whom the petition is brought or the counter petition is made of the nature of the charges intended to be covered by it. There is a provision with regard to deposits for the purpose of making the receipt for a deposit conclusive evidence of the making of it. There is also a modification of the present requirements of advertising the petition, for the purpose of simplifying it. The delays for service and the delays for answer are also proposed to be shortened, and a delay of fifteen days is fixed, after which a day may be fixed for trial. There is a provision that, if neither of the parties choose to have a day fixed for the trial, the court, after the expiry of thirty days, after notification and application by the clerk, may fix a day upon which the parties shall be bound to proceed to trial. Inasmuch as preliminary objections are entirely done away with, of necessity the appeal from any judgment on such objections disappears; therefore the provision in the Act for appeal to the Supreme Court is amended by striking out any appeal from judgment on preliminary

objections. Then there is a provision that petitions shall not abate or be dismissed or withdrawn upon .the death, inability, or withdrawal of the petitioner, and provision is made to enable the proceedings to be taken up and carried on. There is an amendment with regard to prosecutions under the provisions which subject parties to prosecution for offences against the Dominion Elections Act otherwise than by contestation, requiring that any witness that the trial judge indicates as being necessary or useful witnesses on such prosecution shall be summoned, as well as all other witnesses considered [DOT] necessary by the prosecuting attorney.

I do not think the minis

ter understands my question. Every time a complaint is received by the department our officers go to a store and ask for a sample in order that an examination of the article may be made, and if the article is found not up to standard, or deleterious to public health, the law jjrovides that proceedings may be taken against those who are selling it, and we intend to enforce that part of the law.

There have been many complaints in our part of the province, which is a prohibition province, that mixtures are sold in drug stores containing a percentage of alcohol sufficiently large to produce intoxication. I would like to know if the department has taken the proper steps in reference to this matter. It is to be regretted that stuff of that kind can be legally sold by drug stores and licensed vendors of patent medicines to young boys and very often young girls. I am not looking at it so much from the moral as from the physical aspect although both are bad.

No, although I think
Peruna is one. made of Peruna by the Department?
I am informed not.

received?

Do they not get their
licenses for patent medicines in your department?

It is more a certificate than a license. They have to make a certain declaration to the departmeent that the medicine is made of such and such material or liquid, and we give a certificate or a registration number.
Mr. PARDEE. You do not certify as to the ingredients used? Is there no formula that they have to file?
Mr.BLONDIN: No.

If patent medicines containing a large percentage of alcohol and other poisons are sold in these drug stores, it is a serious thing if the law is not sufficiently wide to enable the Inland Revenue Department to have these medicines analysed. The law should be amended in that respect.

I agree with my hon. friend, and it is a branch of the department in which I intend to make improvements this year, and to that end we are providing in the Supplementary Estimates for the salaries of competent officials to analyse these medicines.	.

The Government has no fixed policy on the question ; I believe, on the contrary, that it was publicly stated that it was not the intention of the Government to prevent its employees from taking part in municipal politics?

I thought that it was the very opposite and that by an Order in Council, it was decreed that from the 1st of January, 1916 or 1917, civil servants would be forbidden to take part in municipal elections.
Does that same rule apply to the provincial elections?

I think
the question relates chiefly to the civil servants in the city of Ottawa, and I know that the Government has decided not to interfere.

Has it been brought to the attention of the min's ter that a high-salaried official in his department has written a very severe castigation of the Liberal party in connection with the dual language question in Ontario?

I think that is going
far from tne item under discussion.

No, I think that is
getting very near.
What has my hon. friend to say?

I have this to say. Some days ago I noticed in the papers extracts from a pamphlet which was issued, I understand, by the gentleman holding the position of Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue. I am not bringing up this question for the purpose of making any comparison between
the French and the English languages. Both languages are excellent, and I think no man in this country educated, in the proper sense of the word, who cannot speak both. In this1 pamphlet the deputy minister severely criticises the attitude of the Liberal party in regard to the bi-lingual question. In my opinion he went beyond his depth, and beyond what any deputy minister or civil servant in this country should go. Even the Conservative press, the Ottawa Citizen, for instance,-
That is not the Conservative press.
I know my hon. friend is very sore this morning.
I am not a bit sore. The hon. gentleman has no right to make a statement of that kind.
I will say, then, that the hon. gentleman has reason to be sore with the Ottawa Citizen this morning.
Why?
You had better read it. For instance, that letter addressed to the Minister of Militia that was given to Mr. Brown.
Have you any fault to find with it?
I have every fault to find with it; so has the Citizen.
This pamphlet does not refer to politics in general. It simply refers to the question in debate between the people in the province of Ontario.

Oh, no, it refers to the attitude of the Liberal party on this question, and, in so far as it refers to that, it is not consistent with truth in the way I understand it. The deputy minister makes an attack upon the leader of the Liberal party and upon the Liberal party generally for the stand they have taken on this question. 1 was going to point out that the Ottawa Citizen, which is generally looked upon as a Conservative paper,
Oh, no.

Hon. gentlemen may laugh. If they are willing to read the Ottawa Citizen out of the party simply because of its independence, I cannot help it. The Ottawa Citizen brought this question to the attention of the Minister of Inland Revenue. I really think that the Minister of Inland

Revenue should at least give a lecture to his deputy, not for his attitude on the bilingual question, but for the attack he has made on the Liberal party in this country.

I must tell my hon. frien^l that we do not want to interfere on behalf of or against any group of people in Ontario interested in this question. Just as Mr. Genest and Dr. Freeland and any other public servant in the city of Ottawa has a right to express his opinion, so has my deputy minister a right to express his opinion. I have no responsibility whatever for what my deputy minister writes on municipal or provincial matters, and should not think it just to prevent him doing that, or to lecture him for anything he has done in regard to a question outside of general politics. His pamphlet certainly cannot be called a partisan attack in federal politics.

If the minister says that the pamphlet does not contain an attack upon the leader of the Opposition or upon the Liberal party generally, all I can say is that he cannot have read the pamphlet. If I have read it correctly it is an attack, and was designed and intended as an attack, upon the leader of the Opposition and upon the Liberal party in Dominion politics. The minister is perfectly correct in saying that the hands of the deputy minister or any other civil servant in his department should not be tied upon any question of general interest, but when from one end of the pamphlet to the other an attack upon the Liberal party and its leader is deftly mingled with another question, then I say it becomes a matter of politics and the minister should interfere, especially if he wishes to carry out the policy whidi has been enunciated by his Government from 1911 down to the present, and especially before 1911.
I have nothing whatever to do with that paper. I had in the past, but not now.

I am glad the minister says so. However, they always say that the paper is the organ of the Minister of Inland Revenue; it is known as such; it is accredited as -such; and whenever the minister wants to do anybody any harm it is always through this paper, La Semaine, that he does it. He is so closely connected with it that I do not think I am doing him an injustice when I say that it is his organ.
Mr. BLONDIN; How long is it since this paper was published ?

I could not -say, because I do not read it regularly. It may have suspended publication. -The Tory papers in the district of Three Rivers seem to have been overcome with the sleeping sickness. As soon as the construction of public buildings ceases, the papers dwindle out of sight, and when construction is commenced again, the papers reappear. There was a copy of La Semaine in my box this morning; but, as the minister has said it is not. his paper, I will take -his word for it; and I will tell the people in the riding of Three Rivers to throw the paper aside, because it is not an expression of the opinions of the minister. I will go through the hon. gentleman's riding. and tell the people that he disowns that paper.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext: I cannot read sufficiently well the French language to be able to say exactly what it contains, but I saw an extract from that pamphlet. When the Secretary of State says that the writer did not attack my right lion, friend the leader of the Opposition as such perhaps I agree with him; but will the minister say that he did not. attack the leader of the Opposition as a Liberal, or accuse him of trafficking in this question as a political question? Did he not attack Senator Belcourt, the champion of the French language in the city of Ottawa

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, he attacks him.
-and accuses him of trafficking in this question for party purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That is what he says.
What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It means that Senator
Belcourt is doing what he says he is doing.

It does not mean anything of the kind; it means that this Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue wants to make a political question out of it and wants to make his French confreres of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec believe that the Liberal party are against the French language in this country.

Who made a political
question out of it when they passed a resolution about it in the House at Quebec?

I do not
think the committee are justified in going beyond the point as to whether the deputy minister was wrong in taking part in politics. What he has written I would think would not be a subject for consideration by the committee.

What would constitute
taking part in politics? Would it mean that a man was out stumping? Would a man who would write in a paper making
accusations against another party, a man who- would write pamphlets and circulate them amongst the electors, not be taking part in politics? I submit that when a man writes a pamphlet on any public question and makes that question the pretext for an attack upon a party, the leader of a party, or a body of men because they belong to a certain party, he is meddling in politics. Words will fly, but writings remain. When a man writes a book or a pamphlet and uses any question to serve as a pretext for the abuse and detraction of another party, he is taking part in politics to as great an extent as if he went on the stump and made an attack upon that party. Therefore I think it comes within the scope of the discussion if the pamphlet contains such references as have been alluded to. The hon. the Secretary of State (Mr. Coderre) admitted that the pamphlet contained the statement that the leaders of the Liberal party in Ottawa were taking advantage of this situation to make a political question out of it and that they should be French before they were politicians. The fact that the writer attacks a certain number of men shows the animus and the desire, not to hurt the Liberal party in Quebec, but to hurt the Liberal party in Ontario. That is what he is aiming at. We remember the game which was played in 1911, and we remember that nobody played it better than the hon. the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Blondin). I think that we are within the scope of the item when we discuss this question.

I did not have the opportunity. of hearing the whole of the discussion, but I understand the complaint against the Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue is that he wrote a pamphlet charging that certain prominent Liberals were doing injury to the French Canadian cause and the French Canadian language. I understand the Secretary of State (Mr. Coderre) justifies that attack on the ground that an official has the right to express his opinion by writing pamphlets-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I would like to correct my hon. friend with respect to the statement that I am approving of all that has been said. I said that I had read the book, but that I had not seen anything in it of the character suggested by the hon. member for Cape Breton.

I understand that it
makes a very strong attack upon certain

members of the Liberal party and among others it makes an attack against my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. I "would like to call attention to the fact that it was not so long ago that this Government dismissed from office a gentleman who had occupied a position very much inferior to that of the Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue, who was simply the collector of customs at Coaticook, and who was dismissed because, actuated no doubt by ultra loyal feelings, he wrote a letter to one of the newspapers in which he condemned in very strong terms the conduct of certain Conservative-Nationalists in Quebec who had made the statement on many platforms that French Canadians had only been enabled to breathe the air of freedom by shooting holes through the British flag. That public servant, who had given the very best years of his life to the country, was dismissed without any opportunity of redress or without any opportunity of justifying his conduct simply by reason of having made that statement. The Minister of Customs had only to say that his attention had been called to the matter, and that he regarded it as taking part in political controversy. Without any other reason that gentleman was dismissed from office.

Does the minister say
that every man who does not receive $2,500 a year is getting an allowance of $150, and that that covers all the- employees in the province of Manitoba?
Yes, and in the provinces west.
The custom is, in certain small places, to employ the customs officer to look after the work of the Inland Revenue Department, and the latter department makes an allowance of say $100.
That is the practice.

Does a man who gets
an allowance of $100 a year from the Inland Revenue Department get this $150?

No, this only refers to
the man who receives a regular annual salary.

It does not apply to
those customs officers who receive a nominal salary for doing inland revenue work?

It does not.
Export of electric power, $1,000.

What are the regulations
for exporting electric power?

There are no written
regulations. The application is made to the department and reported to Council.

Under what conditions did
the department give permission to the Cedar Rapids Company to export 60,000 horsepower?

Civil Government-Administration of Justice, salaries, $141,848.75.

Mr. Chairman, I very much regret that the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) should not be in the House, because I am anxious to disprove certain statements he made the other day which are reported at page 1105 of the unrevised edition of Hansard. Here is what he said:
Regarding Hon. Justice Doherty, the member for Laprairie has again distorted the facts; he stated that Hon. Mr. Doherty received a pension of $7,000 a year, while it is only $4,666. I believe the pension of judges has been in existence since 1868.
Now, Mr. Chairman, here is what I had said, as reported at page 913 of the unrevised edition of Hansard:
Is it not his duty as Minister of Justice to make-laws or amend the bad ones? Let him give up his pension; it would be a noble deed; of course, he would be losing $4,666 a year.
That is the statement I made on the 9th of March and the member for Rimouski, before stating to the House that I had distorted the facts, should have read Hansard.
Now, I have another reason to be sorry at the absence of the member for Rimouski, because I wish to make a declaration that concerns him. At the beginning of the session, the member for Rimouski came to me at my seat

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. member that the question now before the committee is the salaries of the employees of the Department of Justice. I suggest to the hon. member that he would be more in order if he would wait and rise to a question ol privilege.

I believe
that what I wish to say is connected with the general question of the salaries of the Department of J ustice and as at the present moment we are speaking of pensions, I think I am entitled to quote the words of the hon. member for Rimouski.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. member that his correction of what the hon. member for Rimouski may have said has nothing to do with the salaries voted for the employees of the Department of Justice. I do think, as I said, that he would be in order if he brought that matter up on a question of privilege. He could then rectify the statements of the hon. member for Rimouski. .
Do you rule, Mr. Chairman, that I would be out of order in quoting the statement made by the member for Rimouski, charging me with misrepresentation?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 maintain the ruling I have just given.

I shall then have to wait for another opportunity. But- since I cannot deal with this question any further, while I have the floor, I will ask the minister if he intends to move to have the payment of his pension suspended during 1915-16?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The question of my pension is noit alluded to in any shape. in the Estimates now before the House. I am not asking any vote to cover the pensions of judges. The pensions are regulated by the law of the country. An Act

would be necessary to amend the law now in force governing pensions, and I do not in the least intend to introduce such an Act.

The minister states an Act of Parliament would be required, but does it not belong to the Minister of Justice to make laws and amend them? 1 say that law is a bad law. In making this enactment, it was in the minds of the legislators to retire those judges who had become incapacitated by age or infirmities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member is not in order in proposing to amend an Act when the subject under discussion is the Estimates, which simply call for a money vote to cover the salaries of the employees of the Department of Justice. This item has nothing to do with pensions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 believe the point of order is well takers I have about me the-best advisers a Deputy Speaker can possibly have, and such is my advisers' opinion. I will point out to the iron, member that the item now under discussion has to do with the salaries of the employees of the Department of Justice and that there is no question whatever of the amount received by the judges who are entitled to a pension. I rule therefore that the point of order is well taken.

Possibly,
Mr. Deputy Speaker, you have about you the best advisers, but I have about me the electors of my constituency who urge me to continue the fight against the present Minister of Justice.
Since it is settled that I may not speak of pensions, I ought to have the right to speak of the assistants who have been given to the minister. First, is it not true that the Minister of Justice, a pensioner of the State, has had to take with him two assistants and increase the salary of his deputy minister to do the work that he himself ought to do, but neglects doing, because he is always absent going to Montreal on his private business, which leaves him no spare time to attend to the administration of the country. I protest against the increased appropriation to pay the salary of the deputy minister and against the appointment of assistants in that office.
Administrate of justice-contingencies,

What was the number of employees in the Depart-

ment of Justice in 1911, and what is it in 1915?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member will find this information in the reports brought down before the House, which give the number of civil servants in each department. The Department of Justice is included in these reports, but I shall gladly furnish any other information required by the hon. member.
Administration of justice-miscellaneous, expenditure, $10,000.
What is that for?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The services covered by this appropriation comprise the following: Cost of administration of justice in the Northwest Territories as now constituted, and in .unorganized districts; expenses incurred in connection with extradition eases and cases of fugitive offenders from or to other parts of the Empire; copies and translations of evidence required in dealing with applications for clemency; expenses of commissions of inquiry; sundry small expenses not otherwise provided for. $10,000 is considered ample to cover the yearly expenditure, but it is impossible to make a close estimate, as in one year there may be a large expenditure under the first two items, and the next year there may be scarcely any. Administration of justice-living allowance for judge of Atlin district, B.C., $1,200.
What is the policy of the'minister with respect to judges holding commissions in the active militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We did have a few applications from judges in different parts of the country asking for leave of absence in order to join the overseas contingents. The matter was carefully considered, and it seemed to the Government that the moment had not arrived when it was necessary that the judges should leave their judicial duties in order to take part in military operations. So far, we have declined to grant leave of absence for that purpose. I think there were altogether four or five such applications.
My question relates more particularly to judges who hold commissions in the militia in different districts, and who at the same time act as judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have had no suggestion that any judge .has engaged in the duties of an officer of the active militia at

times when he should he giving attention to his judicial duties.

It would not be proper
to mention names, hut I know one case where a judge received promotion in the militia of Canada. He was promoted from the rank of captain to a higher rank, that of major or colonel, I think. He says that he wants to go to the front, but the Minister of Justice will not let him go. It seems to me that a man in that position ought either to be relieved of his position as judge, or to be given an opportunity to go to the front and show what he is made of.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the gentleman referred to desires, as the hon member suggests, to be relieved of his position as judge, he has a very simple method open to him. The judicial business of the country must be carried on, even though we be at war. I trust that the time will not be reached when it will be necessary to call upon the judges to abandon the administration of justice in order to take an active part in the war. I am not prepared to say what might happen if some exceptionally well-qualified military man happened to be upon the bench, but under existing conditions we have not felt justified and would not feel justified in allowing a judge leave of absence in order that he may go to the war.
Does the minister not think that a judge who has not the eminent qualifications to go to the front as a militia officer should resign his commission in the militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to know
the details of the particular case in question before pronouncing an opinion in that regard. I might perhaps say something very unfair by reason of my not knowing the particular conditions. It seems to me conceivable that a judge-I do not know whether my hon. friend refers to a high court judge or a county judge-might be able to be of some useful service in connection with the militia without in any way interfering with his judicial duties. I would not like offhand, without knowing the particular circumstances of a particular case, to make a pronouncement upon the subject.

Does the minister remember that last year I had occasion to write to him about the case of a man named Auelair at Riviere du Loup? I never received an answer from the minister. I do not know whether he is too 109
busy with his pension or what it is. I thought at the time that a representative of the people of this country was entit'od to have an answer from the minister, even if he happened to be a Grit or of any othe: political faith. The trouble is that the>i wanted to expropriate a poor old fisherman at the point at Riviere du Loup on account of his political colour, he being a Liberal in good standing. I wrote to the Minister, of Justice asking for fair play and justice to the poor old fisherman. I may say that last session I brought the case to \the attention of the Minister of Public Works and, though we may think lots of things about him, he was kind enough to let me know that he was ready to help the poor fisherman. But I am sorry to say I could not obtain the same answer from the Minister of Justice. Is his heart harder than that of the Minister of Public Works? I hope not. Although I made a strong appeal to him, the poor old man was expropriated while he was away in the bush. His poor wife was alone and they sent down there two sheriffs and twenty young men with axes and picks to dislodge or expropriate the poor wooden building of a fisherman. What did they do with it? They broke it in pieces and threw it into the water, and they took his fishing boat and threw it into the water too. Why? Because he had built on a small piece of land that belonged to the Government at the point at Riviere du Loup. Why? Because he would not vote on the other side. I tell the Minister of Justice that that is a scandal and a public shame on his department and to allow such a thing to be done in a civilized country like ours is a double shame. It is German kultur, it is a German conception, as I said to the face of the minister's own representatives at Riviere du Loup. More than that his representative at Riviere du Loup, Mr. Berubfe,' a Conservative member in the local House, I am sorry to say, told the man that if he would move when winter set in he would allow him to do so. The man promised that as soon as the snow was on the ground he would take his little building away from the Government property. During that time the suit was going on, the fees were piling up and when the snow came the man was sad to learn that he had to pay $72 when he had been promised that if he would remove his property from the Government land nothing would be done. Is that what they call in this country fair play for the poor



fisherman? I leave it to the minister to give me an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am surprised-
Do not be too surprised.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am surprised that the hon. member who feels so strongly for the wrong of this constituent of his, should have been here for something over two months and should never have taken occasion to call my attention to the serious wrongs which he says were perpetrated.
But the wrong is altogether done: you never answered my letter, and I wanted to reach you on your estimates; that is the only way to reach you.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. member did not receive an answer to a letter written to me or to the department, that is a matter which I very much regret. Certainly I have no intention of overlooking the hon. member's letter, and if somebody in the department failed to acknowledge it, I must, on behalf of the department, offer an apology. As to the hon. member's accusations in connection with the manner in which the judgment was executed, I can only say that it is the first time that it has been suggested to me that there was any such harshness. If the hon. member had communicated with me during the time he has been here, I would at least have been in a position to have made inquiries and to have verified the facts. I do not for a moment suggest that the hon. member is not telling the facts as he understands them.
Mr. GAUVREAU I live on the spot and I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But of course there are other people who live on the spot, and there is the counsel in particular to whom the hon. member refers who conducted the case and who I would be surprised to learn had acted with undue harshness. All I can say is that I will look into the question and will try to be as soft-hearted as the performance of the duties of my position will allow.

I am perfectly content with what has been said by the minister. When he has received a report from his attorney down there, he will be satisfied that what I have said is the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

So help him God !
