speechtext:
Well I shall have a statement prepared of what was spent last year and let my hon. friend have a copy.
Exchequer of Court of Canada-salary of Marshal in Admiralty, Quebec, $333.34.
What is the name of the marshal ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand his name is Robert J. Bradley.
Has he a fixed salary or is he paid by fees ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are voting a salary here. I understand that he also gets fees for certain proceedings.
Did he get any fee in connection with the Storstad ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am really not in a position to inform the hon. gentleman.
Exchequer Court of Canada-to Chas. Morse for furnishing reports of Exchequer Court decisions to legal periodicals, $50.
To what periodicals does Mr. Morse furnish these decisions ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand to legal periodicals, to law journals and things of that kind. I can get the list if my hon. friend desires it.
No, I do not want the list. But Mr. Morse is the editor of the reports, and I suppose he gets any benefit that is to be derived from the sale of them. I was wondeiing what the $50 was for.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken in supposing that Mr. Morse gets the price the reports are sold for. He gets his salary, but that is all. Whatever the reports are sold for is turned over to the Government, as I understand.

The minister is mistaken in that. Mr. Morse is the editor of these reports. I wanted to know how much Mr. Morse pays the Government for the printing. Mr. Morse is the editor of these

reports and sells them at $5 a piece. It is not much of a practice to supply them to the law publications.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman quite certain that he is not confounding Supreme Court reports with Exchequer Court reports?
Quite certain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall verify what my
hon. friend has said.

I have tried to get them myself. As the Exchequer Court reports were printed by the King's Printer, I thought I could pay for them on time and get other advantages, but he would not sell them under any circumstances. He sells them only to the editor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There may be some arrangement for the sale of them.
Administration of Justice-Yukon Territory- travelling allowance of judge, $500.
How many judges?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Only one.

Well,
travelling is expensive for him.
Administration of Justice-Yukon territory- Maintenance of prisoners, $10,000.
How many prisoners?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The amount that is voted is to cover the expenditure. The prisoners, I understand, average nine at the same time. The expenditure under this head in 1912-13 was $7,946, and in 1913-14 $6,558.

How many jails are
there?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is a jail at Dawson and a jail at Whitehorse. I do not know but that the Mounted Police building would be used for the detention of prisoners when necessary.
Dominion Police, $128,765.

When will we be
allowed to discuss the items on page 35 in regard to the salaries of the chief justices?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The items on page 35 are provided by statute, and I am asking no votes for them.

I wish to ask the minister if he has had any representations made to him in regard to an increase in the salaries of county court and district judges,

and if he has any policy to announce in regard thereto?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have had some representations made this year, but not the usual crop, if I may be allowed to use the expression. It has not been considered that this was a desirable time to deal with the question.

The expenditures on page 33 of the Estimates are apparently authorized by statute also, and I presume there will be no vote asked for them here. I would like to ask the minister if, in connection with these local judges in admiralty, he has ever considered the possibility of doing away with the system of court procedure at present in vogue which makes it necessary that alb actions in admiralty be brought in some of the admiralty courts and whether all these actions could not . be brought in the High Court and thus do away with this so-called admiralty work. It is a misnomer, it is quite a useless procedure, it is extra expensive, and the whole legal profession and litigants would be glad to see it done away with. Matters m admiralty could be brought into the High Court to much more advantage to litigants and with much more convenience to solicitors than they can toe disposed of under the system at present in existence. I took this matter up with the former Minister of Justice, Sir Allen Aylesworth, and I understood from him that in consequence of some old system which existed in the eastern provinces, and because there were some admiralty judges who were receiving $1,000 a year, it would not be well to make the change at that time. But surely the niue has come when we can do away with this effete system of procedure and have all these cases brought into the High Court and disposed of under the High Court procedure.
I will be glad if the Minister of Justice would give this matter some consideration because I know full well that it is a question which interests the profession as well as litigants. It would be well to have the old system done away with.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall certainly be happy to look into the matter to which my hon. friend has referred. It is the first time it has been called to my attention since I have occupied the position which I now hold. I have some recollection of the matter having been brought up under a previous administration. At that time there seemed, at all events in the Montreal district, to be

a very strong desire for the maintenance-of the present system. I was not, however, sufficiently concerned with it at that time to go into it with enough care to form any very definite opinion as to whether the system should be maintained or not, but I shall be glad to take the first opportunity of looking into it.

I want to say a word about the appointment of the registrars of alien enemies in my county. On February 11, I asked the following question:
Is Hyman Benjamin, of Glace Bay, N.S., employed by the Militia Department or by any other department of the Government? If so, what are his duties, and what is his salary?
The answer is that he is " not in the employ of the Government." I knew that this young man was in the employ of the Government, and on March 17 I asked:
1.	Who are the registrars of alien enemies for the riding of South Cape Breton, N.S. ?
2.	What is the salary paid to each?
3.	What assistants have they got, and what are their names and salaries?
4.	What are the names of the interpreters in connection with the work, and what are their salaries?
Mr. Casgrain (for Mr. Doherty) :
1.	H. C. Moseley.
2.	$200 per month.
3.	D. Nicholson, $100 per month; A. D. Gillis, $100 per month; B. Morrison, $30 per month.
4.	H. Benjamin, $75 per month.
The registration of alien enemies in my county is, in my humble opinion, not conducted in a desirable manner. Under the Order in Council of the 24th December, 1914, the city of Sydney was made a registration district, and it is in that district the the persons mentioned in the answer of March 17 are acting. Until the appointment of Mr. Moseley to the city -of Sydney district at $200 a month, the work was being done all through the county of Cape Breton, including all the mining towns as well as the city of Sydney, by Mr. D. A. Noble, who is the head of the police force of the Dominion Steel and Coal Company. Mr. Noble and his assistants were doing this work to the entire satisfaction of Colonel Sherwood, chief of the Dominion Police, and they were doing it without pay. When it came to the appointment of a registrar under the new regulation, Mr. Noble made application, but he was told that while he had been doing the work well the position was going to some one else, and witn that I cannot find fault if the Government so determined. But if the registrar, who has his jurisdiction limited to the city of Sydney, is entitled to receive
pay, surely Mr. Noble, who had spent money out of his own pocket in connection with his duties, and his staff, were entitled to some recompense. Mr. Noble is, as a matter of fact, doing the registration work in the county of Cape Breton to-day, outside of the city of Sydney. Mr. Noble and the others were perfectly willing to do this work as loyal citizens, without compensation, but if the department appoints a registrar under salary, surely Mr. Noble and his officers are also entitled to the same treatment. This young man, Hyman Benjamin, against whom I have nothing to say, is getting $75 a month as interpreter for Mr. Moseley, and that is looked upon as a joke down there. He is competent to speak English and Yiddish, but he does not speak German or Austrian, and, as a matter of fact, any person who lives there will tell the minister that he is not looking after these duties at all, but that his work is in another direction. I do not wish to be personal, but I would ask the minister to investigate this. When I put a question on the Order Paper, asking what assistants Mr. Moseley had, I was under the impression that Sergeant Stephen Black of the city of Sydney had been Mr. Moseley's assistant since the office was opened, but that information was. not given in the answer, although I believe it is correct. When in February last I asked if Benjamin was in the emplpoy of any department of government, I got the answer he was not, and when, having put the question in another form, I was told he had been in tlie employ of the Government since January 3, such a reply makes one suspicious. I have no objection to officials getting fair remuneration for their services if they do the work, and I have always maintained in this House and elsewhere that civil servants were entitled to a fair salary, but I do object to men being paid for ostensibly doing work when they are not capable of doing that work. I also object to a man getting a salary of $200 a month for doing work which had been done up to the 3rd of January for nothing by others, and who are still doing the same kind of work in the county of Cape Breton and getting nothing for it. I submit this matter to the Minister of Justice in good faith. Mr. Noble is not looking for pay, but he feels that if Air. Moseley is entitled to $200 a month for looking after alien enemies in Sydney, and the work being practically completed by Mr. Noble on the 3rd of

January when he left that office, that he is entitled to compensation. I have no reflection to cast upon Mr. Benjamin, of Glace Bay; he is a nice young gentleman, but he is not qualified, and if he were he is not doing the work he is paid for; he is engaged in other work the nature of which I do not wish to make public. These matters have been brought to my attention several times by persons of both political parties in the county of Cape Breton, and I submit them to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to the error which
seems to have occurred in the answer as to Mr. Benjamin being employed in any department of the Government, I can only explain it by the fact that the question as first put specially mentioned the Militia Department, and attention was not called to it as having any reference to the Department of Justice. When the question was put to the Department of Justice, it was answered correctly, which shows, of course, that there was no intention to mislead in any way. Mr. Noble, under the direction of the Chief Commissioner of Police, did do very considerable work, under the Order in Council first passed, but later on, when the Order in
4 p.m. Council establishing a system of registration officers became effective, it was represented to us that in this district of Sydney there was a very large number of persons of alien enemy nationality, and that there was necessity for establishing a registry office, taking in the whole district. Not very long after that we ascertained, as the hon. member states, that Mr. Noble had been acting for the greater part of that district, and we then restricted the jurisdiction of the registry office to what we believed to be a portion of the district that had not already been dealt with by Mr. Noble.

That is the city of
Sydney?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Mr. Noble had done exactly the same work at Sydney as he has been doing throughout the county.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose was to restrict it to that portion of the district which we understood had not been fully attended to, but there may have been a misunderstanding about that. I do not know what arrangement was made between Commissioner Sherwood and Mr. Noble, but I shall

inquire into it, and I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Carroll) that there is no desire to avail ourselves of the services of anybody without paying proper remuneration. The representations made to me are to the effect that Mr. Noble's work was well done. I think I may say that the work in that registration district is practically completed, and that it is probable it will not continue very much longer. As to the competency of this young gentleman referred to by my hon. friend, this is the first time my attention has been called to the matter. When we adopted the system of appointing registrars, we asked suggestions from the military officers commanding, and I think that was done in the Maritime Provinces. We then asked the registrar to select his assistants, and under that system it may be-and I have rio doubt the hon. member is satisfied it is so-that unfortunately the gentleman selected for the position he referred to is not competent. I regret very much if it should be so. I shall inquire into the matter and if the facts are as stated I shall certainly take means to rectify it.

The same work had been done by Mr. Nobld in the city of Sydney until ithe passing of this Order in Council and afterwards until the 3rd of January, as had been done before. The alien enemies are thickest in the mining 'districts, such as New Waterford, New Aberdeen, Dominion and Bridgeport. There were more alien enemies in New Waterford than in the whole city of Sydney. It *was a surprise to the people of Sydney generally that there should be a register established at Sydney, where Mr. Noble had done all the work as well as all that had been done in the other mining districts.
Can the minister give us an idea of the number of alien enemies who have been interned, where they have been located and what work they have been put to, if any?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The camps and stations where the aliens are actually interned are at Halifax, Quebec, Montreal, Toronto, Kingston, Petawawa, Spirit Lake, Kapus-kasing, Brandon, Lethbridge, Vernon and Nanaimo. In addition to these, two camps have been organized-one in the Port Arthur district for 800 prisoners and one at Amherst for 500 prisoners of war now on the way from Jamaica. The total number interned at the different, places

that I ''have enumerated. i3 2,752. The prisoners in Montreal,' who number only 100, are not at work; they are being detained there for the present, getting ready to be moved on.
Are they in the old jail?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, they are not in the jail at all. No prisoner of war that I know of has been put in any jail building. They have been detained-I might almost say in a luxurious building, but at all events, in a building that was provided for the detention of immigrants on St. Antoine street, Montreal. It. is a new building, and we have endeavoured as far as possible to (provide for the comfort of the men. The three principal camps are now Petawawa, where there are 573 men, Spirit lake on the Transcontinental, in . the province of Quebec, where there are 683, and Kapuskasing in the province of Ontario, where there are 438. At Brandon there are 246, at Lethbridge 120, at Vernon 68, and at Nanaimo 97. At Spirit lake and Kapuskasing the men are at work clearing land. The respective provinces of Ontario and Quebec agreed to give to the Department of Agriculture a tract of land in each case of 1,000 acres or thereabouts, which is ultimately intended to be used as a model farm. We have established a camp at each of those two places, and the labour is being utilized in the clearing of the land. Furthermore, we look forward to quite a number of those people settling, under the ordinary provincial laws providing for the taking up of homesteads, in the neighbourhood of the particular locations. It seems to us and it also seems to the provincial authorities that, handling the matter in this way, we are doing a benefit to the locality, a more immediate benefit to the province and an ultimate benefit to the country generally.

In regard to the matter of which I was speaking before, Colonel Ingram was registrar at Sydney, and before he went to the front, he had as his chief assistant Bertram Ingram. Mr. Moseley was instructed to keep on the staff that Colonel Ingram had there. He kept them all on but Mr. Bertram Ingram, Colonel Ingram's assistant. After Mr. Moseley had been in office some days, Bertram Ingram was advised by the department that his services were no longer required, and that another gentleman by the name of Gillis, a quite capable man,
*was put in his place. Why were Mr. Bertram Ingram's services dispensed with ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There was no particular reason. As I said a moment ago, we adopted the policy of allowing the registrar to secure his own assistant. Colonel Ingram was the first registrar, and the gentleman referred to was a relative of his. There is no reflection in that at all. When Colonel Ingram went to the front and his position .became vacant, Mr. Moseley was appointed. I was informed that Mr. Moseley was allowed the privilege of appointing his own assistant. Those positions are not considered as permanent, because it is only temporary work. At the outset, it seemed to us that for this temporary work, if the gentleman were a suitable person to be appointed as registrar, probably the most satisfactory way of getting the work done would be to allow him to appoint his own assistant. The functions of the office will be terminated very shortly now. The termination of Mr. Ingram's appointment was due to the fact that Mr. Moseley coming In, availed himself of the privilege given to him of securing his own assistant.
I understood Mr. Bertram Ingram got his dismissal through the department at Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can ascertain that. The matter came before me in some connection. If I am not mistaken, the hon. member or some one else asked me a question on the subject. Speaking from memory, I may say that, Mr. Moseley having communicated to us his action in the matter, we, who had been paying the salary of Mr. Ingram,- felt it proper to communicate to him the fact that a change had taken place.
Expenses of litigated matters connected with the Department of Justice, $13,000.

The creation of the office of Solicitor General of Canada was the result of a desire to avoid the payment of large fees to outside counsel in connection with the business of the Department of Justice. When Sir Charles Fitzpatrick was Solicitor General, he took briefs for the Crown in the Supreme Court and in the Exchequer Court, and he did save a considerable sum of money e_aeh year during which he held office as Solicitor General. Nowadays, however, -the Solicitor General does not take briefs in court or attend to the legal business which was had in view when the office of Solicitor General was first established. I am not blaming the

present Solicitor General any more than the Solicitor General under the former Government, but it is my opinion that the whole object of the establishment of the office of Solicitor General has been overlooked. The position has become a political one. It is a necessary position; the Solicitor General may have duties to perform in connection with the executive affairs of Government, but the office does not exist as a department of Government in the way that it existed when it was first established. The idea that the Solicitor General should take briefs for and act, one might say, as senior counsel for the Government, thus effecting the great saving to the Treasury of Canada which was the object of his appointment. I should like to know whether we are ever to return to the original conception of the duties of this office, or whether the Solicitor General is to continue as a political appointee and not as a useful member of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman had kept as close an eye on the Solicitor General as he would have us to understand he did, he would have been aware that the Solicitor General has attended to quite a number of important things for this Government, and I am glad to have the opportunity of recognizing his valuable services in that regard.
In what cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We will ask the hon. Solicitor General to give a list of them, if the hon. gentleman desires it. The hon. gentleman should not have spoken quite so soon without being certain of "his information. I think it would be perfectly fair to point out also that since the office of Solicitor General was originally established, there has been a very; considerable increase in the work to be done in' connection with the administration of justice in the different departments. If one looks at the increase in the number of applications for release under the Ticket-of-leave Act, one will realize at once that there is a great deal more than one man's work to be done in that connection. I do not think I make any mistake in saying that within the last, three or four years the increase has been from 75 to 100 per cent-more nearly 100 per cent than 75. In that connection the Solicitor General has rendered most valuable service, and wherever else there may be room for criticism in connection with the department,
I think the hon. member selected certainly the least vulnerable point when he

selected the Solicitor General for the subject of his attack.

Surely the hon. Minister of Justice does not suggest that the high capabilities of the Solicitor General should be devoted almost exclusively to considering applications for tickets of leave. A junior clerk could attend to that part of the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member will allow me to differ from his opinion in that respect. I think there is no more important work in connection with the Department of Justice than the matter of advising His Royal Highness with respect to the exercising of clemency. I am glad to have the abilities of the Solicitor General devoted to it, and, besides, I myself, have always felt it my duty to give quite a considerable amount of time to the matter.
Will the minister tell the committee something about the methods employed at present in connection with the ticket of leave system?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In dealing with tickets of leave I do not think it is possible to lay down any absolute rule that any convict who does a particular thing or things will get a ticket of leave; one has to be guided very largely by the circumstances of each case. One important factor in determining whether the crown should be advised to exercise clemency is whether the party has one or more offences to his charge. The conduct of the man while in prison is a factor, though, perhaps, not as important a factor as the one which I have just mentioned. The circumstances of the case are reported to us by the judge before whom the applicant was tried; sometimes we have the advantage of reports from the prosecuting counsel or from some other persons who are in a position to give us valuable information with regard to the particular circumstances of the case. Then we have the services-and they are very valuable-of the parole officer, who in a large number of cases makes particular inquiry as to the antecedents of the person concerned and as to circumstances connected with his offence that may not have come out at the trial. We endeavour to give in each case the proper weight to each one of these considerations. Of course, the fact that a man is a first offender is in itself a consideration of very great importance.	.
We have to consider the period of time for

which the man has been sentenced, the 'period he has served, and so forth. I think it would be difficult to hv down a policy on the subject. The policy. that we have tried to follow involves careful examination of each particular case, and in each particular case we endeavour to give our best consideration' and soundest judgment to those circumstances which make for or against the exercise of clemency.
Is it the practice of the department to give a ticket-of-leave after a certain number of years to a man under a life sentence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have given tickets-of-leave to men who have been under life [DOT] sentence. In that connection of course we have had to take into consideration all the different circumstances to which I referred a moment ago. I do not know that there was ever an absolute policy that a man under a life sentence should under no circumstances obtain a ticket-of-leave. I do not think there has been any change from the practice that prevailed before we came into office.

I did not know whether the path of error that had been blazed by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) was to be followed by other hon. gentlemen opposite. I have had reference to the Act establishing the office of Solicitor General, which was passed in 1889 I believe, and have noted the purposes for which the Act was passed and the duties there laid down on the incumbent of the office. The duties are simply described as "to assist in the work of the Department of Justice." Surely it will be^manifest to the hon. member for Welland that there are many ways in which that work can be assisted besides taking part in the litigious work of the department I observed my hon. friend to say that the practice which was established in 1889 of the Solicitor General taking cases for the Government into the courts of Canada had fallen into disuse and become utterly extinct. From what information I have I am very much disposed to agree. I have understood that it became extinct, like many other good practices, under the late Government, and I am of the opinion the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) will confirm what I say in that regard. However, it has met with a revival. Since I have had the honour of holding that position and have had time, I have endeavoured to the best of my capacity to do some service for the department and for the country in the way of conducting cases.
Mr. DEVL-IN: Did you win any cases?

I will answer the hon.
member for Wright (Mr. Devlin). The late Government, in the course of their conduct of affairs, took occasion to expropriate certain property near the city of Winnipeg. The late Government made an offer of a certain sum for the property, but it was refused by the owners. The Government-entered into no negotiations, as a prudent man would have done, with a view to purchasing the property-and I believe it might have been purchased then-and, as a consequence, a heavy problem devolved upon this Administration, namely, the settlement of the damages for that property. It involved a claim in the Exchequer Court against the Government of Canada-the largest claim, I think, that has ever been made against the Government. It involved a suit that in length of time and legal difficulties involved will compare very favourably, I think, with any suit that has ever been brought in the Exchequer Court. Necessarily there would be a judgment against the Government but perhaps it would satisfy even the hon. member for Wright himself if he succeeded in securing a judgment which was only about 5 per cent of that demanded by the complainants. So that if he considers a 5 per cent judgment against the Crown a successful issue on the part of the Department of Justice, then I can claim a success.
In other words, you lost the case.

In other words, the
hon. member for Wright holds that it is the duty of the Crown to take the property of individuals and pay nothing for it; that unless the Department of Justice succeeds * in enabling the Crown to defraud the people of this country, the Department of Justice loses its case. But that is not the attitude we assume. We believe we got a judgment according to the law and a fair judgment; so successful, indeed, that the other parties to the suit have entered an appeal and notified us that they purpose proceeding not only through the Supreme Court of Canada but to the Privy Council in England. We do not feel so-badly over the judgment that we have appealed against it. There have also been other cases, but I need not go into them in detail. I do not think the course we have pursued is under challenge. I

know the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) is now convinced that the very good practice that was once in vogue has been revived under this Administration. I know that he regrets he did not make his complaint when there was cause to make it, and when he might have done a service to his constituency and to the country. The other work, as the minister has stated, has grown at a great rate. Indeed he has underestimated the rate at which the applications for parole have proceeded. They are now more than double what they were in October, 1911, and are still increasing. The number that daily comes before us for adjudication is about fifteen, and that of course occupies some little time. At all events it will be my stern endeavour to live up to the duties imposed upon me to the best of my ability, and I trust that if I set a good example in that regard the hon. member for Welland, when in good time he reaches this post, will strain his energies to the uttermost to follow the same creditable course.

Rather than regretting
that I brought up the question I am rather pleased that I did so, as I can now more strongly justify the assertion that I made. Whatever the statute may say as to the duties, the fact remains that the position of Solicitor General was created for the reason that I stated so much legal work was being done by outside counsel that it wras thought in the interests of the country that a Solicitor General should be appointed to act on behalf of the Crown in all cases which came before the Supreme Court or the Exchequer Court. The salary of the Solicitor General was fixed at $4,000 a year, he being also a member of the House with a sessional indemnity of $1,500, as it was then. But this Government has raised the position of Solicitor General to the dignity of a minister of the Crown, with a salary of $7,000. Is not that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. member is mistaken again.
Is it still $4,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is $5,000, as it always was. We have not raised it in any event.

Very well. The Solicitor General has not indicated any cases that he has conducted in court except the one in connection with the expropriation of land in Winnipeg. The duties of the Solici-
tor General were to be to take cases in court for the Government and so relieve the Treasury from the payment of large counsel fees to outside counsel. These counsel fees are still being paid and are continually increasing, and the Solicitor General at the present time is not performing the duties for which he was originally appointed, that is, to take cases in court and to look after the business of the Government in court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can only express my regret that Parliament did not prescribe as the hon. gentleman says was the intention. That may have been the intention of my hon. friend, but Parliament left it to the discretion of the Department of Justice how best the services of the Solicitor General might be availed of.

How many cases
has the Solicitor General , pleaded since his appointment, and in what courts?

The Department of Justice has under review continually a very great number of cases in very many of which the Solicitor General himself takes a part, if not in the actual conduct of the case in court, in the preparation of the case and in the various legal discussions that necessarily are entailed. At the present time I have under my actual conduct, I think, four distinct cases. I do not interest, myself in all cases. I do not think it is within the capacity of any man to interest himself in all. [DOT]
Supposing the Department of Justice has a case in the Exchequer Court, the Supreme Court, or the Privy Council, who is to fight the case before the judges?

Usually the Deputy
Minister of Justice.

The Solicitor General
seems to credit me with having locked the door in the Solicitor General's office and closing up business when I went in there. When I left, I did. I am not going to enumerate or go into details, I shall just refer him to Mr. Justice Cassels for information as to how many cases I took in the Exchequer Court.
We shall have him before the Bar of tne House.

Of course you cannot : -certain this from the records, because the

name of the Attorney General appears on the record in every case.

Since the
Solicitor General is so energetic-and I know he is energetic in whatever field he is working-I would bring to his attention the case to which I have already referred twice during the session-those of the landowners at Valcartier who have not yet been paid the money due them in connection with expropriations. The Militia Department informed me the other day that all the cases which have not been settled have been referred to the Department of Justice. I brought to the attention of the House a letter from the solicitor of several of these people whose lands had been expropriated and who have not yet seen the colour of the money of the Government; I brought up letters asking why the Government, since they have not paid, cannot institute proceedings at once. The first letter was sent to the Government on the 9th of November, but on the 10th of this month no process had been issued. I bring these facts to the attention of my hon. friend, in the hope that he will take this matter up himself and have it attended to at once.

I shall be very pleased to look into the matter in the department. I trust, if the result is a satisfactory settlement, that my right hon. friend will not follow the example of the -hon. member for Welland and complain that it is not taken into court.
That is not very satisfactory. This is the third time I have been told by occupants of the Treasury benches that they will be pleased to look into the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This time I might follow it up. This minister is pleased to say that he has been very pleased to look into the matter, and has given instructions that it be proceeded with so far as the papers are in his department and without any delay whatever, and that it be verified whether all the papers have come or not. I iva-s not present when the right hon. gentleman raised the question the last time. I had the advantage of seeing his observations in Hansard, and I gave those instructions. My hon. friend the Postmaster General says that a number of cases have been quite recently settled. That would be done through the Department of Militia.

My complaint was that these cases should have been settled not recently but long ago, and it has been simply by calling the attention of the House and the Government to the fact that at last something has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in a position to control precisely what matters did come to our depai'tment for action; but I can say that when they did come, in some of the cases it was found that there were difficulties with regard to the titles that had to be cle.ared up. Before the right hon. gentleman raised the question my attention was called by a memorandum to the fact that the titles of some of these parties, ostensible owners, required to be looked into.
The cases I drew to the attention of the House were not delayed on account of insufficiency of title, hut of disagreement as to the amount to be paid.

Has the minister any personal knowledge of an information taken to expropriate land-at Nicolet for a wharf? I read some time ago in the Star that the 6um of 5450 had been offered to the Episcopal corporation of the diocese of Nicolet for a certain piece of land which had been refused; that proceedings -had been instituted by the Crown, and had come in conflict with certain laws or canons of the church which put the Attorney General in the position of a man who would be excommunicated if he proceeded with the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I need not express the intense alarm with which an intimation of possible excommunication coming from such a high ecclesiastical -authority as the hon. member for Three Rivers inspires me. I am all the more terrified that it comes at the very outset and for the first time from him.
It came from the Star, your organ, which is a higher authority than I am.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not the -advantage of controlling that particular twinkling orb. I might say that I am not aware that any suggestion such as the hon. gentleman indicates has been made; it has not come to my personal knowledge. My recollection is that an effort was made to secure a property, but as there was some objection to it being taken I understood that consideration was given to the possibility of providing an

equally convenient wharf at another place. We would seek, in locating a wharf in any locality, to place it where it would he most suitable and convenient and give rise to the least inconvenience to the people of the district.
I do not want the minister to lead the country and the House to believe that I am taking the lead in this case and acting as an ecclesiastical authority.
They would not believe it.
I hope they would not believe it. I feel sorry for the minister, coming down from the bench and then being excommunicated. My authority is the Star. I think I can produce the clipping.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not excommunicated yet. I will inform him when it comes.
Expenses under the Pecuniary Claims Convention with the United States, $25,000.
I would ask for some information upon that. Have some these claims been settled?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There has been adjudication upon a certain number of claims but I am not aware that there has been any actual settlement or payment made. It is anticipated that when a number have been decided there will be a settlement.
Penitentiaries-Kingston, $210,600.

The last report of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is for the year ended March 31, 1913. I regret that the report for txie fiscal year ended March 31, 1914, is not before us; therefore, I will have to take what is available. The report which I have in my hand gives the population of the various penitentiaries in Canada as 1,970. The population, I presume, has gone up to the 2,000 mark within the last year. It is worth noting that this report states that the increase in the number of convicts in our penitentiaries in the last ten years has been 56 per cent. It is also worth noting that the increase in the number of Canadian-born convicts in the last decade is only 10 per cent. I would like to call the attention of the committee to the fact that taking the convicts in our various penitentiaries per 10,000 of each nationality, the number is only 1.75 for Canada and 8.7 for the United States and a3.3 per cent for Italy. The-figures are to my mind very startling. I also want to direct attention

to the fact that there are in our various penitentiaries 229 convicts under 20 years of age or about 10 per cent of the total population Of tne penitentiary. There are 875 convicts between the ages of 20 and 30 or a little over 44 per cent; 55 per cent of the present population consist of convicts under 30 years of age.
The increase in the number of our convict population seems to me to indicate beyond any doubt that the system which does at present, and has for years, prevailed in -regard to the administration of our penitentiaries whether under the late Government or under the present Government has been a failure. Some weeks ago I placed a question on the Order Paper asking for certain information in regard to the penitentiary at Portsmouth. The answer to this question would seem to me to be an endeavour to convey the idea that things at the penitentiary at Portsmouth had. very greatly improved in the last three months or since u.e investigation which was conducted a short time ago. I believe that there has been improvement in one or two respects at least. For" instance, I do not think there have been any insane convicts subjected to the tubbing which had prevailed to a certain extent previous to the investigation, The minister says himself, in answer to one of my questions, that there has been no hosing of convicts since the investigation and that it is under consideration as to whether it will be done away with or not. But, Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding one or two changes of this character, I think that the general conditions prevailing in that institution-and I dare say the conditions are very similar in the other	institutions-are	very
much the same as they were before the investigation was held. I regret to express the opinion that, if that is true, it is true largely oecause the commission appointed to investigate did not investigate as thoroughly as it should have done, In order that the committee may understand that there is a general opinion throughout the country that conditions are not what they should be, I am going to quote at some length from editorials in various papers published in this province and in the province of Quebec. I shall quote from papers on both sides of politics. The Kingston Standard, Montreal News, Toronto Globe, Toronto News, Hamilton Herald, Hamilton Spectator, London Free Press, Ottawa Free Press, London Adver-

tiser, and others, have taken up the matter and with one accord they condemn the existing conditions and deplore the delay in righting those conditions. I want to place on Hansard some editorial opinions from some of these papers-and let me say that these editorial utterances were published just a short time before Parliament assembled this year and long after the report of the investigating committee was brought down. The Kingston Standard says editorially:
So long1 as sick men are treated more like animals than like human beings, it can scarcely he said with truth that they are receiving justice in the fullest and largest sense of the word.
And again:
The stone pile still holds out-that infamous place of refined torture where men are not only breaking stone but are -breaking their hearts as well-a place where the finest intellects are stunted and finally deadened and where hopes are blasted and buried for ever.
And again:
As a matter of common humanity it desires to emphasize that the sooner action is taken the better.
The Toronto Globe refers to:
The barbarous and indefensible treatment of prisoners in the Portsmouth penitentiary for a year after an official report made the public familiar with what was and is being done in their name and with their sanction.
Again:
On every citizen rests the responsibility of seeing that the disgraceful conditions disclosed by the inquiry at the Portsmouth penitentiary are remedied.
Again:
It is impossible to believe that the public are indifferent to appeals against the degrading, brutalizing, disheartening processes that stunt the mind as well as cripple the body. The stone pile is still there a monument to governmental incompetence. The colossal stupidity of the men on whom it imposes as a pretence of productive labour is incomprehensible. It certainly does not impose on the dullest convict. He sees he is not working productively, but is subjected to a dreary and crippling routine that serves to deprive him of the results of effort, dull his senses, dwarf his mind, kill his ambition, and fill him with undying resentment at a cruel and protracted wrong.
Again, from the Toronto Globe:
Restriction of correspondence to one letter every two months is another unexplained infliction. It suggests a determination to prevent the incarcerated from being reached by humanizing influences.
Again, from the Toronto Globe:
The commission dimly comprehended the fact that it was dealing with one of the deepest problems of organized society. It revealed enough
to prove the existence of cruel and stupid wrongs against the imprisoned. It is strange and even lamentable that the report has been received in official circles with an almost childish distortion of vision. The feature of disclosure that impressed official authority was not the partial drownings, not the shocking hospital conditions, not the lack of medical attendance, but the fact that some employees had understated their ages when applying for appointments. The treatment of the imprisoned is an accurate measure of the governmental conscience.
Again, from the Toronto Globe:
Some one must champion the men whose sufferings are intentionally inflicted by organized society and whose complaints are unheeded. While such things continue the men on the outside of our prisons are in deep disgrace, whatever may be the verdict of the world on the imprisoned.
The object of Doctor Edwards, and of all who aid in this needed reform, is to end a notorious crime on the part of organized society, not to embarrass or cast reflections on any Government, minister or official.
I want to say that for that last sentence 'of the Toronto Globe I want to express my thanks. This leading Liberal newspaper of Canada has, I think in that sense, been more just and fair to me than those ffom whom I might naturally expect fair treatment. The London Free Press says:
It is a reflection upon the humanity of Canada when it is stated that even sick men at this institution are treated without consideration. Apparently the idea prevails at Portsmouth that the aim and purpose of a penitentiary is to break men. Brutality that does not stop short of the inadequate care of the sick; that drives men to the daily task of breaking stones as a punishment and that refuses to the convict all knowledge of his loved ones save once in two months is unworthy of this free country.
The Ottawa Free Press:
The utmost cruelty exists in the administration of the prison hospital at the Portsmouth penitentiary.
The London Advertiser:
While there is much talk about the abolition of capital punishment it is questionable if it would be less cruel to end the lives of some of the men who are sent into Canada's jails and penitentiaries than to allow them to he brutalized and deprived of every fine quality.
And again it refers to the penitentiaries:
As these dreary criminal universities where a man comes out with a higher degree in crime than he could ever secure In the loose unorganized school of the open world.
Again the London Advertiser states:
They (the convicts) should not be handled like delicate pieces of china but they should be given a chance to square accounts and not to be transformed into moral, mental and physical ciphers.

The Toronto News:
Prisoners, it is said, are treated more like animals than human beings. Surely this is a longstanding abuse that should be removed.
The Montreal News:
Our system of prisons is admittedly archaic and improvements competently suggested ought to be made.
The Hamilton Herald:
The evidence taken discloses revolting conditions at that institution-unnecessarily harsh treatment of prisoners as a matter of system, brutalities perpetrated by individual officials, the enforcement of a policy of repression which must have had the opposite of a reformatory effect. There was also disclosed the fact that there had been undue favouritism in the appointment of minor officials and discrimination in treatment against some.
Again:
You will never reform a criminal by cruel treatment. More probably you will succeed only in confirming him in his criminal tendencies.
The above are from very recent edi-. torials, and I have taken them from what I think I may safely call the leading newspapers of this country. Their opinions should, it seems to me, receive very serious consideration., I want to add another extract, from the Toronto Globe, which on November 3rd last said:
Many convicts in Canadian prisons are willing to enlist and take their chance in the war rather than serve out. the terms to which they have been sentenced. Kingston's recent investigation, although handicapped by the terror and reluctance of ex-convicts, revealed conditions from which an ordinary man would naturally turn to the worst horrors of war without the slightest promptings of patriotism. Torturing, tauntings, goadings, annoyances and the dreary routine with tortures awaiting every overflow of the goaded spirit must create p mental condition ready to welcome any change.
As I have said, these are extracts from leading newspapers of the country.	I
believe there are crimes which are not recorded on our statute books, crimes of organized society against those who have violated the laws of society. I want to say right here and now that I believe the conditions in our penitentiaries are, to say the least, deplorable. My sole object is to see an improvement in these conditions that will give the men who are
5	p.m. unfortunately incarcerated,	a
chance to make good in this world. That is my object.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is quite a while since I first took this matteT up. It is over three years since I first drew the attention of the Minister of Justice to the conditions at Kingston penitentiary. It

was on the 2nd of December, 1912, that I made certain 'Specific charges against certain of the officials of that institution. On the 25th of August, 1913, 18 months after I had made my charges verbally and 9 months after I had made these charges in writing, a commission was appointed to investigate the charges I had made and the general conditions obtaining in our penitentiaries. Speaking on this subject a year ago, I made my comments in regard to that commission, and I drew attention to certain parts of the evidence which warranted me, I thought, in saying that the commissioners had deliberately falsified and misrepresented the evidence they had taken. I feel so certain and strong of my position in that regard that I would say that if I cannot easily establish from the evidence that was taken that they repeatedly misrepresented the evidence in their report to this House, and in some instances absolutely falsified the evidence in that report, I would be willing to resign my seat in this House and Tetire from public life forever. That is, at least, an indication of how certain I feel in making that very strong statement. I shall not go over in detail the various Instances to which I referred last session, but there aTe some things to which I want to refer, and to which, in justice to myself and to my object, it is my duty to refer.
Will the hon. member be good enough to give the names of tl ese gentlemen who have falsified the evidence ?
The names of the commissioners, they being the gentlemen to whom I refer, are: G. M. Macdonell, J. C. Downey, and Dr. Etherington.
Is my hon. friend so certain that the evidence has been falsified and falsely reported by the commission that he is willing to give up his seat in order to support his contention?
Are you sorry for it now?

If my hon. friend will possess his soul in patience, he can draw his own inference from my remarks as I go along.	I want to say further that
in supporting Colonel Hughes for that position, I had pretty good encouragement from many sources. He was supported by a large number of hon. members from the province of Ontario, sitting on this side of the House. He was supported by a number of members from the Ontario Legislature on the Conservative side. He was supported by several Conservative associations passing resolutions. He had been recommended by men high up in the Department of Justice in this country in the past. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, Sir Oliver Mowat and others, who had been Ministers of Justice in Canada had spoken very highly of Mr. Hughes, and Mr. Hughes had been in the penitentiary in one capacity or another for twenty years. All that was sufficient to warrant me in feeling that he would fill the position of warden very successfully. Mr. Hughes, in the course of his seeking for that position made charges against certain officials of the institution. What he said was largely, though not entirely, the basis of the charges which I made against the deputy warden and against the surgeon, and subsequently against the hospital overseer. His information was corroborated by information given to me by others. WTien Col. W. S, Hughes was inspector and came before the commission to give evidence, I was very much surprised at the first sentence which fell from his lips in reply to a question from me. He said to me: "I am not going to tell all I know about the Kingston penitentiary."

I was somewhat surprised, and asked him why. He said "I am now Inspector of penitentiaries, and I am not going into details in connection with that institution." Later he went into the box and took the usual oath to tell the truth, and the whole truth. I call attention to the following paragraph appearing on page 7 of the last report of the Minister of Justice:
During the past year-
That is, the year when this investigation was going on.

the penitentiaries have been subjected to more than the usual quota of criticism. It is needless to state that fair constructive criticism is welcomed and helpful, and receives careful consideration. by those engaged in the task of administering penal institutions. There is a class of criticism, however, which is merely the parrot-like reiteration of the mis-statements of officials who have violated their oath of office, or the equally unreliable vapourings of ex-convicts who seek notoriety. Such criticism is unfair and injurious. There is no close season -to protect officials from such attacks. They can do so only in their annual reports.
This is signed by the two inspectors, Douglas Stewart and W. S. Hughes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I notice that my hon. friend, perhaps inadvertently, mentions the report as being that of the Minister of Justice. He has, however, pointed out that it is signed by the inspectors who made the report.

I thank the minister for the correction. I merely read from the cover of the report, which states that it is the report of the Minister of Justice as to the penitentiaries of Canada. No fault is to be found with Inspector Douglas Stewart in connection with the writing of that paragraph. I have not the slightest doubt but that Inspector Stewart felt that he could have made that language a good deal stronger. But what do hon. gentlemen think of W. S. Hughes signing his name to that report, a man who, more than anybody else and more than all others put together, has violated his oath by giving out information in regard to that institution? Last year I said that in my estimation there was discrimination along religious lines; that, either consciously . or unconsciously, favouritism was shown by the deputy warden. What authority did I have for making ithat statement? I had in the first place the authority of a return which was brought down in the House in answer to a question which I put to the Secretary of State. In this return the information is given -that a few years ago seven out of the ten

keepers were Roman Catholics, and that of 20 disciplinary officers some 14 or 15 were of that particular faith. That is why I made the statement that it appeared to me that there was favouritism or discrimination. But that was not all. I have in my hand a statement by Mr. Hughes, which he himself prepared for me right here in this building, in room 16, and in which he gives me.some information in that connection. He has furnished me also with a list of his various qualifications for the position which he was seeking. He had a letter which, when I first saw it, I thought was a spontaneous outburst of admiration for Mr. Hughes on the part of guards and ex-guards of Kingston penitentiary. Later, however, I found out that the letter was prepared by Mr. Hughes himself; that all the adulation which was therein contained was the work of his own pen. In addition to that, I have certain statements which Mr. Hughes made with regard to officials in the penitentiary. I have been represented as being actuated by improper motives; as going round with a bowie knife in my belt ready to take the scalp off any person not entertaining the same religious beliefs as I do. I am trying to live that objection down; I hope that not many members of this committee hold that opinion of me. However, I am going to give one of the remarks made by an inspector of the peni-ientiary in regard to one of the officials of the penitentiary; it is in the statement which Mr. Hughes kindly prepared for me. Mr. Hughes says that Rev. Father McDonald, the Roman Catholic chaplain of Kingston penitentiary, in addressing the prisoners in the chapel of the penitentiary, said that " any one who said he was saved outside the church of Rome is a liar, a scoundrel, and a fakir." These are not my words; they are the words which Inspector W. S. Hughes says were used by Father McDonald, the Roman Catholic chaplain.
Was that written in room 16?

It makes no difference
where it was written. I have said that it is a statement made by Mr. Hughes, who makes this comment in regard to the statement which he places in the mouth of Father McDonald:
This was spoken from the pulpit in the prison, and should show very plainly where the trouble arose.
Inspector Hughes refers to the mis-statements of officials who violated their oaths

of office, and also to criticisms of the penitentiaries. A certain guard of the name of Smith was suspended for not attending to duty. In his report Inspector Hughes finds fault with officials because of their violating their oaths of office-and it is a violation of his oath of office if an official writes to anybody outside about matters affecting the penitentiary. Inspector Hughes says that Smith got a raw deal in the matter of his suspension. I have other letters from the gentleman, but will not take the time to place them on Hansard. I think that I am justified in letting the committee understand the position which Mr. Hughes has occupied in the past. I have not any particular reason to be proud of the course the commission took; my faith in humanity was not strengthened by their course. It was not until after I came to know and understand Inspector Hughes that I fully realized the import of the words used in one of Shakespeare's plays:
You have among you many a purchased slave,
Which, like your asses, and your dogs, and mules,	.
You use in abject and in slavish parts,
Because you bought them.
'Mr. Hughes's salary as accountant of the penitentiary was very different from his salary as inspector of penitentiaries. I do not know whether the salary had anything to do with Mr. Hughes's attitude. But I know that a man by his name who a year ot two ago was drawing a salary of 11.700 is to-day drawing a salary of $3,700 as inspector of penitentiaries and about $7 or $8 a day as colonel of the 21st battalion. In the course of my remarks last session I had to refer to Deputy Warden O'Leary, Dr. Phelan and hospital overseer Wilson. I made certain charges against those men, and I made those charges because I thought it was my duty to do so. I do not believe that, no matter how earnest and sincere the present Minister of Justice may be in his desire to rectify conditions at the Kingston penitentiary, it will be possible for him to rectify those conditions with those men holding the offices that they do. Others may differ from me in that regard; but I am stating my belief and, holding that belief, I think I should put before this committee certain reasons why I think these men are not fit for the positions which they occupy.
I shall not refer at length to the commission issued to the three gentlemen at Kingston. I have already said that in my judgment it was a mistake to appoint two 110
men or even one man on that commission from the city of Kingston, for reasons which appear to me to be obvious. These men were well acquainted with the officials involved, with the friends of those officials; and it was asking a good deal of citizens of Kingston to expect them to be in every respect entirely fair. I also think it was a mistake to appoint Mr. Downey, an official of the Ontario Government, as the third member of the commission. It seemed proper to the minister to place a five-year limit on the instructions that he gave to the commission. I have said before, and I say now, that I do not think that was fair to me; certainly it was not fair to me as it worked out. The minister may argue that he intended the commissioners to disregard the five-year limit as far as. my charges were concerned. The fact remains that they did not see fit to disregard the five-year limit, and I was placed in the unfortunate position of making certain charges -which the commissioners would not investigate at all, which they ruled out entirely. I think it would have been a little kinder if it had been intimated to me that they did not want to go into some charges which I had made; in fact, they might have been deleted-left out of consideration altogether. For instance, I made a charge of perjury against Deputy Warden O'Leary. This went away back to sixteen years ago. That charge was never investigated as the commissioners say it was. That was one of the misstatements they made. I say that charge was never investigated. In their report they say it rested only upon the unsupported statement of ex-guard Patterson. That also is incorrect, because before that commission, in the presence of eight or ten people and under oath, Inspector Hughes said that if the 'deputy were to receive a sentence of three years for every charge of perjury he could prove against him, he would spend the rest of his days behind the walls. That statement was made before the commission. I want to give some additional reasons why I think O'Leary'is not a fit and proper person for the position he holds, and why it is not in the interest of reform that he should remain at that institution. I think I suggested some time ago the desirability, so far as the wardens and deputy wardens and Certain, tother heads and officials of our penitentiaries are concerned, that they should be appointed, not as the warden or deputy warden of a certain institution, but as a warden or deputy warden of penitentiaries; and I



would repeat that, in my judgment, it would be advisable, even with the best officers, to transfer them at times from one institution to another. I believe it would have a good effect, as there is a tendency for these men to get into a rut if they remain for a long time in the one institution. I said that Deputy Warden O'Leary had shown evidence of a callous indifference which unfitted him, in my opinion, for the office he held. For instance, he made the remark to a guard that he should let a convict hang, but wind his clock; that was of more importance than anything else. The commission in their report attempted to show that that statement was not correct; but we have evidence in the report, we have the statement of Greer as to what took place. Greer swears that the deputy reprimanded him for being late in winding his clock. When he explained why he was late the deputy passed the remark: "Let the man hang, but wind your clock!" The commissioners read into Greer's evidence something which Greer's evidence does not contain. They say that Greer stated that he was on duty in 1907, and that the prisoner whom he cut down, had died two years before that, and that therefore Greer's statement was wrong. That was not fair. Greer in his evidence states that he would not attempt to give dates in regard to that or any other occurrence. He said he was on permanent night duty for eleven months previous to finally leaving the institution; but he said nothing about not being on night duty temporarily at various times. I have an affidavit from Greer which I think I should place on Hansard, because his honour and his word have been questioned by the commission. He says:
I,	Samuel Greer, of the city of Kingston, in tile county of Frontenac, make oath and say:
1.	That I was a guard at the Kingston penitentiary from October, 1895, to September, 1907.
2.	I gave evidence before the Royal Commission and was questioned as to an incident that happened during the time I was a guard, j stated that I could not give the date of the occurrence, and could not give any dates for happenings, and had no records of anything that happened while I was on duty.
3.	That I was on duty in the asylum at night, and when on my rounds to wind the clock and make inspection, I found a convict named Bishop hanging to the bars of his cell. X went at once to rescue him and succeeded in bringing him to life. The time occupied in reviving Bishop made me late in winding the record clock, and I was asked by Deputy Warden OT,eary why I was late, and I told him I had been rescuing a convict who was hanging in his cell, and he said that if I found any convict hanging again to attend to my clock first and

that the conviot would not hang while I was winding my clock.
4.	I reported this to Chief Keeper Hughes, who is now Inspector Hughes, and he told me that any time I saw a man in danger to save life first at all hazards, and he would see that I was protected.
S.	J. Greer.
Sworn before me at the city of Kingston, in the county of Frontenac, this 20th March, A.D. 1915.
Geo. H. Smythe,
A commissioner, etc.
I have also here testimonials from Mr. Hughes, from O'Leary himself, and from ex-Warden Platt, speaking in the highest terms of Greer's efficiency and reliability. If that was only one instance, perhaps it would not be worth citing, but that is not the only instance. Subsequent to that, another guard named Mar,sh found this same convict attempting to commit suicide.
By the way, you wdil find corroboration of what I have said in regard to Greer on page 417 of the evidence, and in regard to Marsh on page 658 of the evidence. That information is not given in the report of the commission, but I will give it now. Marsh found this convict hanging. Remembering how Greer had been reprimanded, he left the convict hanging, went out and wound his clock, and then came back and cut him down. I am informed they had considerable difficulty in bringing him to. That is only another instance of the callousness of the deputy. Guard Aiken (page 394) stopped in his rounds to pick up a sick convict who had fallen out of his cot and vomited on the floor. He helped him into liis cot, cleaned up the floor, and then wound his clock. This made him late, and he was reprimanded for being late by the deputy, who said that it was not his business to look after the sick convict. I cite these three instances as indicating, to my mind at least, a callousness and indifference on the part of the deputy which unfits him for the position he holds. The minister may think differently, and of course he will act upon what he thinks.
In regard to hosing. A certain cell was constructed specially for the purpose of hosing, that is, the corners of the cell were rounded off so that the victim could not get away from the action of the water. The hose has been used on convicts at different times at a pressure of 60 pounds to the square inch, and I believe that Inspector Stewart said that at St. Vincent de Paul Penitentiary the pressure was even as high as 75 pounds to the square inch. The report

of the commission in regard to this may be found on page 18. It says:
The victim must cry out for mercy or suffer physical collapse. But as a disciplinary agency it should he ranked with the rack and the thumb-screw, cruel and inhuman.
That is the opinion of the commission in regard to hosing. On page 17 we have this extract from the report: "The convicts who were hosed describe the punishment as terrible." On page 17 Ex-Warden Platt says:
In his evidence the doctor said he did not like hosing, and he never ordered it again.
He only used the hose once and never used it again. On page 18 of the report Inspector Stewart says:
The hose succeeds where nothing else will. It never fails to beat an incorrigible convict into submission. Very few men who will not give in in 30 to 60 seconds.	[DOT]
Q. Is that the most severe punishment?-A. No, I think shooting is more severe.
On page 17, referring to hosing, this commission says that , it should be ranked with the rack and the thumb-screw, cruel and inhuman. But on page 24 this same commission, in its desire to exonerate the deputy, says:
No act of his was revealed that indicated he was either cruel or inhuman.
And yet the deputy is on record as using the hose five times. Hosing is part of the punishment which is allowed under the regulations, and it would not be right or fair for me to blame the deputy for those regulations. Ex-Warden Platt tried it once and never used it again. Apparently he did not like it. The point I am endeavouring to make is this. The commissioners say that hosing, as a means of punishment, is cruel and inhuman and ranks with the thumb-screw and the rack; yet on the next page these same commissioners endeavour to exonerate the deputy from any act of cruelty or inhumanity, although he had actually used the hose in five cases.
Let me refer again to tubbing. The report on page 12 says:
There was evidence to show that insane patients had been punished by tubbing. An attempt was made to explain away the tubbing as a necessity where the victim were in a filthy condition and refused to bathe. It was made abundantly clear to your commission that the tubbing at Kingston penitentiary was resorted to neither for sanitary nor therapeutic reasons, but as a punishment.
That was in the commission's report. An attempt was made to explain away this 110J
tubbing on the ground that it was enforced bathing. A short time ago I placed a question on the Order Paper in regard to both hosing and tubbing. The answer to my question will be found on page 548 of Hansard of March 4 this year. I asked by whose order or direction' the act of tubbing insane convicts was carried out. I did not get any answer to that question, but there was what purported to be an answer. It said that bathing was enforced in cases where the convict refused to take a bath. That is not what I asked at all, but that is the answer I got. I further asked:
Are there any guards or other officials at Portsmouth penitentiary who have assisted in or ordered the tubbing of insane convicts?
To that question I was given what seemed to me a rather remarkable answer-an answer sent, no doubt, from Kingston penitentiary at the request of the minister. The answer was:
The warden is unable to find any one on the staff of the penitentiary who has any knowledge of tubbing having been used except as before described.
That is an enforced bath. It goes on:
The following are the statutory declarations of officers who are still on the staff of the prison and who have been, from time to time, in charge of the insane ward:
Then follow four or five affidavits, and let me point this out in regard to the affidavits which were given in connection with the answeT to my question. Guard Madden was in charge from the 31st of December, 1907, to 31st of August, 1911. Then we have McConville in charge from July 3, 1911, to September 13, 1911. So the affidavits of these two men conflict, because both Madden and McConville swear they were in charge during the months of July and August, 1911. If you look carefully at the affidavits you will also find that apparently there was no one in ehaTge from May 25, 1913, to July 1, 1913. That time is not covered at all. And further. Apparently there was no one in charge from September 8, 1913, to November 11, 1913. I should also like to call attention to this fact. The warden says that he was unable to find any one on the staff who knew of tubbing as a punishment. In regard to that I would respectfully draw the attention of the warden to Bryant's evidence to be found on page 789. Bryant says he helped to tub. But Madden, who furnishes an affidavit, here says that no such thing took place. Bryant says in his evidence under oath that both Madden and McQuade were

present when this tubbing took place. I also want to refer to Babcock's evidence on page 796, McWatters' evidence on page 804, and Matthews' evidence on page 816, and if the .sworn testimony of all these is not sufficient, we might look at the sworn evidence of Dr. Phelan, who said under oath that he had heard rumours that tubbing was taking place in the institution, and had put up a notice that it be discontinued. What does Bryant say in his evidence on page 789:
Q. Who would give that order? A. By the authorities.
Q. Who would that he? A. Either the warden, the deputy warden or the doctor.
Q. Give the names of some of them who were there? A. Mr. Madden was keeper.
Q. Would he be present? A. Yes.
Q. Anybody else? A. Mr. McQuade would be present.
Take the evidence of Babcock on page 796:	,
Q. Ever see a prisoner put in the tub to give him a cold bath? A. Yes.
Q. Where was that? A. Asylum.
Q. By whose orders? O. Mr. McWatters.
Q. What office did he hold? A. Acting keeper, I think, at the time.
Q. Why was the tubbing done? A, He insulted another officer.
Q. The prisoner had insulted an officer. A. Yes.
Q. Then the tubbing was done for punishment. A. It was.
Q. Who besides yourself were present when the tubbing was done? A. Just the three of us: McWatters, Matthews and myself.
Take McWatters' evidence at page 804. He says:
Do you remember Matthews being with you and Babcock in the asylum on duty together seven years ago?-A. Yes.
Q. Do you remember a convict having insulted Matthews and being subjected to the cold tub as punishment for the insult?-A. Yes, I do.
Q. You would not have subjected him to that kind of treament if it was only for the purpose of making him clean?-A. I would not.
Take Matthews' evidence at page 816:
Q. Were you present when he was put in the tub?-A. Yes, sir, I was present.
Q. Why was he put in the tub?-A. Misbehaviour, of course.
Q. What was it?-A. Well, the misbehaviour was this: he threatened to strike me.
Q. He did not need a bath because of his dirty condition?-A. No.
Q. It was.because of what he said to you that he was given a bath?-A. Yes.
