speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman mind mentioning the time that happened?

Counting back from the date when this evidence was taken, I think

he said it was seven years ago. I dare say that the minister has thought that I have been very much misinformed in regard to certain facts, but I think I have had better information than the minister has had. For instance, in answer to my question the other day, it was stated that:
The hose has not been used since May 11, 1913.
If you look at page 823 of the evidence given by Charles Grey, you will see that Grey says that the hose was used in his presence in July, 1913. That shows very conclusively that information supplied to the minister in regard to this matter was not reliable. I also want to call your attention to the fact, in regard to hosing and tubbing of insane convicts, that Dr. Etherington, at the time the commission was holding their investigation, declared that there were two insane convicts confined in the prison isolation. These prisoners should not have been there. There is a ward for them. The evidence also gives us verji clearly the fact that a convict was sent from Dorchester to Kingston because Kingston is the only penitentiary where they have, or are'supposed to have, facilities for taking [DOT] care of insane convicts. This man was sent from Dorchester and committed as insane? He was not committed to the insane department of the institution as he should have been, but ' to the prison. These conditions, I think, . call for some redress and some action on the part of the department.
I further charged that the deputy had shown favoritism in assigning guards to the various posts. I gave reasons why I made that charge a short time ago. The commission in their report referred to the evidence of one or two witnesses, as far as favoritism was concerned, and referred to that evidence as if it were all the evidence along that line. Allow me to call attention to the evidence of guards McQuade, Montgomery, Smith, Aikens, Bannister, Bryant, Caughey, Davis, Johnston, Ingledew, Patterson and Inspector Hughes, all of whom swore that the deputy showed favoritism. Consider their evidence, and let the minister, or any other person, judge for himself as to whether the evidence does indicate, consciously or unconsciously, that the deputy did show favoritism, which was not in the best interests of discipline. I charged him with neglect of duty and lack of judgment. Take the case of convict Chartrand. Let us see what Dr. Platt said in regard to that on April 12, 1912. He was warden then. He said:
v\

A convict designated as dangerous andv marked for special care escaped under circumstances which force one to the conclusion that wrell known, important and imperative duties were either neglected or performed in a culpably perfunctory manner.
The minister reflects on " the insufficiency of right surveillance provided " and concurs in the censure of warden and deputy. Where did the deputy show lack of judgment? McConville was in charge during the day time and a man named Smith was the night watchman. This prisoner was marked as one requiring special care. Who was McConville? McConville was a man who formerly had been suspended for being asleep and drunk on duty. The convict who cut the bars in the corridor which enabled Chartrand to get out said before he died that the time he cut these bars McConville was asleep in the corridor. The result was that the escape took place. It was only a partial escape as the convict did not get altogether outside. Smith was the night watchman. Who was Smith? Smith was a comparatively new man who had been reprimanded fourteen times for neglect of duty during a few months, or probably a year and a half, before that. Am I right in saying that the deputy, whose business it is to assign the various guards to their positions, showed a lack of judgment in placing in charge of that particular ward, where there was a convict that he had instructions particularly to watch, a man who had been suspended for being drunk and asleep on duty and another man who had been reprimanded fourteen times for neglect of duty.
I say that in my judgment O'Leary is absolutely tactless. He shows lack of tact in placing boys on the stone pile. He shows lack of tact in permitting men like Travers to have certain privileges which are not allowed to other convicts. A convict comes to the institution-a boy it may be 14 years of age. The deputy warden assigns that boy to his work. Surely, Mr. Chairman, if there is any convict who should receive special consideration it is the young lad of 14, 15 or 16 years of age who, unfortunately, comes into the institution. It is claimed that there is not enough work for all classes. That is very true and it is not to the credit of this Government, nor was it to the credit of the last Government, that nothing was done along the line of recommendations made by the Inspectors Douglas Stewart and G. W. Dawson that more productive labour should be furnished for the prisoners. But, Sir, surely a man of proper judgment, when a young lad like
that would come into the institution, would place him in the tailor shop, or the shoe shop, or where they are making the brooms, or at some work where he would learn something. The last place they ought to put him at is the stone pile.
Surely every person.will agree to that. I say, Sir, that if there, was only one thing connected with the institution which shows the absolute inefficiency and inability of O'Leary for the position he holds, it is the fact that he repeatedly has placed small boys on the stone-pile, which in my humble opinion, furnishes evidence that he is entirely unfit for his position.
I want to call attention to one or two other things that this man O'Leary has done. The prison records show that two convicts named, I think, Taucob and Quinn, were caught by Guard Walsh committing an unmentionable and abominable offence. Now, Mr. Chairman, a crime committed inside the walls of a penitentiary is supposed to be punished as it would be punished if it were committed outside the walls of the penitentiary. The guard did his duty in reporting that crime and giving certain details of it in writing to the acting warden, who, at that time, was Deputy Warden O'Leary, and Deputy Warden O'Leary- you will find this also on record-notwithstanding the denial of these convicts, believed they were guilty of the offence with which they were charged. Although I am not a lawyer, I believe I am right in saying that when a crime is committed inside a penitentiary the person committing that crime is to be taken before a judge and tried. Why was that not done in this case? It was not done, and why? These men, had they been brought before a judge, would undoubtedly have received a sentence of a number of years for the offence they committed, and which was charged against them by the guard, and which the deputy warden said he believed they were guilty of, and yet this deputy warden took it upon himself to act as judge and jury, and he sentenced these two men to a year in the prison of isolation. Is that the proper kind of a man to be practically in charge of that institution? Carlyle says:
Show me the man you honour; I know by that symptom better than any other what kind of man you are yourself, for you show me what your ideal of manhood is, what kind of a man you long to be.
I say, Sir, speaking my own opinion, that Dan O'Leary is not the kind of man I

would honour with that position or any other. The evidence is beyond dispute.
That O'Leary showed a callous indifference even to the risking of human life.
That he repeatedly took part in punishments which the Royal Commission rank with the rack and the thumb-screw, as cruel and inhuman.
That he was either aware of and endorsed the tubbing of insane convicts, or showed his utter incompetence by not knowing of that horribly cruel and utterly indefensible torture being perpetrated under his very eye.
He can get on either one of these horns which to him has the blunter point, but he cannot get rid of both. He says he did not know anything about the tubbing of insane convicts. I say that if he did not know he ought to know or he is not fit for the position he holds, and if he did know he is not fit for the position either.
I charge that consciously or unconsciously he exhibited a favoritism to his co-religionists, which was detrimental to the discipline of the institution, and which was responsible for much of the lack of harmony.
I say that he repeatedly neglected his duty. I say that he allowed special privileges to some and was cruelly exacting with others, and I say that he has shown complete unfitness by his general lack of judgment, in assigning convicts to their work, to wit, putting boys on the stone-pile.
That is my indictment against Deputy Warden O'Leary. I do not care who is appointed Deputy Warden of Kingston penitentiary, but I do say this: that when the warden of that institution is a Protestant, and the warden of that institution always has been a Protestant, I do believe and have so stated that I think the 'deputy warden should undoubtedly be a Roman Catholic, whoever he may be who is appointed there. But, I think he should be a very different man from what Deputy Warden O'Leary has shown himself to be by his conduct in the past. There is only a minute or two Before six o'clock, and I would like to submit a question or two to the minister which he can take up during recess.
At six o'clock the House resumed and then took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

I do not undertake to forget that; I would be forgetting my duty if I did; but

Before recess I had stated why, in my opinion, the present deputy warden of Kingston penitentiary was not a fit and proper person to occupy that position. It is incumbent upon me to make a few references to Dr. Phelan, the surgeon of that institution, against whom I preferred certain charges, which charges were also dealt with b'fore the Royal Commission. I charged Dr. Phelan with having used violent and indecent language. I shall not quote his language, but I refer any person who wishes to read his words to page 389 of the evidence. For evidence in support of that charge, reference may be made to pages 419, 420 and 421, evidence given by guard Redden. In considering the charge of using indecent language, the following questions were put and the following answers given:
Q. What did he (Phelan) say about the conversation that took place between Aikens and himself at the gate?-A. He said I could say I had not heard it, and I told him I could not say that, that I had heard some of it.

Q. Dr. Phelan suggested to you that you should say that you had not heard the conversation?-A. I told him I could not say that because I had consulted him.
Q. You knew there was to be an investiga,-tion?-A. Yes.
Q. Did the doctor say there was to be an investigation?-A. He said he understood there were charges made against him.
Q. And what did he ask you to do about it? -A. He did not want me to do anything about it.
Q. As far as that case particularly, he wanted you to say you had not heard it?-A. *He said I could say I had not heard it, but I told him X could not say that.
Q. You did not assent to that?-A. No, sir, no.
That was not disputed by Dr. Phelan, who was represented by probably the ablest lawyer in Kingston, Mr. John L. Whiting. I recognize Mr. Nickle's ability, but I guess I shall have to hold to my original opinion. Mr. Whiting is the ablest lawyer in Kingston, and Mr. Nickle is an exceedingly close second. The evidence very clearly indicates that Dr. Phelan was endeavouring to induce Reddin to go on the witness stand and, so far as the matter which was being investigated was concerned he was trying to induce Reddin to withhold his evidence-trying to induce Reddin to perjure himself.
Another charge which I made against Dr. Phelan was in regard to graft. He said he took fees for examining guarus to which he was not entitled. Dr. Phelan as physician has certain duties. Among those duties is the examination of any guard appointed, and he is paid a regular salary for doing that. He is not supposed to get any money out of the guard for performing that service. The commissioners in their report at page 25 say:
Dr. Phelan admits that in four cases he asked for and received a small fee from an applicant for a guard's position as to his physical fitness, and this is a contravention of the statute, as he is not to practise his profession. He says he has not done so for several years. The amount wrongfully taken by him was $4.
The commission have not dealt candidly with that matter. Four cases were proven, they were satisfied that the charge had been proven ana requested us not to take up any further time by bringing forward other cases. He does not say and we have no right to conclude that because we had proved he had taken and he admitted having taken $4 from tour different candidates that it had stopped with that; indeed, guard Reddin, at page 441 of the evidence, says that Dr. Phelan asked him for a fee when he came. He did not pay the fee, but Dr. Phelan told him that he most generally
got a dollar for examination. Now, that may strike some of you as a very small affair, a matter of $3 or $4. The amount was small, but if Dr. Phelan would take money in that way from guards to which he was not entitled, contrary to the statute, he is at least open to the suspicion that he might take much larger fees for doing other things that he should not do. For instance, a suspicion has gone abroad that men of wealth who have become convicts in prison have prevailed upon the prison surgeon to report their health as breaking down under confinement. It has been stated that wealthy men or men who had wealthy relatives have paid prison surgeons, I do not say Dr. Phelan, for reporting them as breaking down under confinement and in that way have induced the surgeons to make representations to the Government that these persons should be liberated because their health was failing and if they were kept in confinement they would die prematurely. In that way they have been released before the termination of their sentences. Take the case of a man named McRea confined in Kingston penitentiary,, sentenced for life for manslaughter. He served only nine months of his sentence. He was released because, in the first place, the surgeon of the penitentiary, Dr. Phelan, reported that his health was entirely breaking down. Another doctor was called in from Montreal to corroborate that and the man, after serving nine months of a life sentence, was set free and is at liberty to-day.
I want to refer to another thing:	Dr.
Phelan's manifest neglect of duty. Rule 52 of the regulations states:
Upon the arrival of a convict the surgeon shall examine him to ascertain whether he is affected by any putrid, infectious or cutaneous disease whether he labours under mental or boclily defects, and whether he has been vaccinated. He shall report the facts to the warden.
Did Dr. Phelan carry out that rule? He made no attempt whatever to carry out that rule. Man after man was brought before the commission who swore that he had not been examined, until the commission said: " It is no use taking any further evidence on that point." They were convinced that the rule had not been lived up to. Then, take rule 53:
The doctor shall give special attention to the hygiene and cleanliness of the prison and prisoners, ventilation of the dormitories, workshops and other buildings, and to the water supply and drainage.	,	!

No person, after reading even a small portion of the evidence, would say for a moment that Dr. Phelan attempted to live up to that rule. That was the second rule which he openly disregarded. Why, Sir, in regard to the water supply, sixty or seventy men would be working on the stone pile; the drinking water for those men would be in the one pail and only one cup would be provided for them to drink from; and it was clearly brought out in evidence that there were men among that sixty or seventy who had loathsome diseases. One of them had syphiletic sores in the mouth, and still he was drinking from the same cup that was provided for the sixty or seventy others on the stone pile. Yet we have Dr. Phelan in his report saying that so far as the hygiene and cleanliness of the prison was concerned it was all that could be desired. He made reports like that year after year.
Did he attend to his work properly? Look at the asylum. Forty insane patients in the day-time were herded together in one common room-the violently insane and those not so violent all herded together. In this building they had night buckets for the excreta and the stench in that building was simply horrible. If you want further confirmation of the last statement take what Dr. Young says. Dr. Young, assistant superintendent of the Rockwood asylum, at page 10 of the report, testified:
* The physical condition of the patients (in the insane ward) shows the effect of improper diet, insufficient exercice and fresh air.
Each patient is locked in his cell without proper sanitary conveniences from 4 p.mf. to 7 a.m. The door of each cell is simply a grating and there is no provision for the isolation and care of noisy and filthy patients. There is no provision for the proper classification of patients, all of whom are gathered together in a large day-room, the acute with the chronic, the old and helpless with the impulsive and violent, the lucid with the demented.
That is what Dr. Young says. What does Dr. Platt say? In his report of 1908 I find these words:
The medical superintendent-
That is Dr. Phelan-
-who is prison surgeon, makes a huried call once a day, Sundays excepted. This constituting the whole care and treatment of the criminal insane.
Let me read an extract from the commissioners' report, page 11:
Many an unfortunate must have been deprived of a fair chance of recovery by reason of the State's unpardonable neglect. Further we find that the insane inmates have not received the attention which their state demanded 
and in some instances they have been subjected to unjustifiable punishment.
On page 12 the commissioners place the responsibility for this primarily on the surgeon and the inspector, the surgeon's annual reports giving the impression that the state of the insane left nothing to be desired, and the inspector accepting from year to year the existing conditions without adverse comment. I believe that Inspector Douglas Stewart said that it would not have made any difference if he had made adverse comment, as no attention would have been paid to him anyway. To show that what I have quoted in regard to this matter is absolutely right, let us take an extract from Dr. Phelan's report to the Government. He says on page 31:
The sanitary condition of the prison for the year has been up to the usual standard of efficiency.
It is a mighty low standard.
Every effort has been made to leave nothing undone which should be done to carry out the principles on which these important measures are established. The various workshops, dormitories and other departments are carefully attended to as regards ventilation, heating and cleanliness.
And this with 70 convicts drinking out of the same cup, from the same pail, and some of them with loathsome diseases 1 And yet he says the convicts are carefully attended to as regards cleanliness.
The water used for drinking purposes was examined during the year, and found free from organic particles which would cause disease.
I wondered if he examined the water in the pail I spoke of a moment ago. He says:
As usual, the hospital has been kept in a good condition, and always ready for the reception of the sick, who receive every attention, day and night, the directions being carried out most carefully.
Let us see if that is true. On page 17 of their report the commissioners say that there is no effective ventilation in the hospital, no sanitary appliances except an obsolete bucket for excreta, and that the only equipment for operating purposes is an old wooden table, that old books covered with dust lie on the floor, and that the place is generally dirty. The commissioners say:
Under no conditions are the patients permitted to have exercise in the fresh air nor indeed to leave their cells for any purpose.
Yet the surgeon's report says that everything is lovely, things could not be better, the hospital is kept in good condition, with everything always ready for the reception of

the sick, when the operation is performed on an old wooden table, when dusty books litter the floor, when there is any amount of dirt in the corners! Yet the hospital is in splendid condition and always ready for the reception of the sick. That is what the surgeon says. In that institution for the sick open wounds of . convicts have been dressed by convict orderlies who knew absolutely nothing about dressing wounds, who simply pulled out the dirty and rotten batting that was used, and tore off the dressings with their hands and put other dressings on without any antiseptic precautions whatever, being taken. That is the condition. Convicts suffering, lying awake in pain at night, and, as the evidence clearly shows, no person going to their assistance. The hospital overseer, H. W. Wilson, who was appointed by this Government, has refused time and again to get out of his bed to attend to the wants of sick convicts. It was amply proved before the commission that he refused to get out of his bed, although he had been provided with a room in the hospital so that he might be within call in case of emergency.
I think there have been some changes made in that institution since the commission held their investigation, and if I had anything to do with bringing about that investigation-I think possibly I had, at all events I am credited with having had something to do with it-I am very glad that we have succeeded at all events in stopping the tubbing of insane convicts. If I have done nothing else, I have cause to be gratified.
Let me now summarize in regard to Dr. Phelan. Did he use violent and indecent language. He admits that he did. That charge is proved. Is a man who would use violent and indecent language in speaking to one of the guards the proper kind of person to be surgeon of that institution? Did he try to induce a guard to perjure himself? Look at Redden's evidence on page 420 and you will see that clearly proved. Did he graft by taking money that did not belong to him, whether it was $4 or only 4 cents? He admits that he did. Did he persistently day by day and month by month disregard rules 52 and 53? The commissioners say that he did disregard these rules. Did he give only a small part of his time to the inspection, diagnosis and treatment of sick convicts? The warden of the penitentiary says that he did. Is it true that many an unfortunate insane convict was deprived of a fair chance of recovery because of Dr. Phelan's unpardonable neglect? The commissioners, on page 11 of their report, say that many an unfortunate convict was deprived of a fair chance of recovery. That every opportunity was given for the spread of loathsome diseases because of his disregard of rules 52 and 53 is amply shown. He paid no attention to hygiene and cleanliness, and his annual report from which I have quoted is, to say the least, most misleading. Yet Dr. Phelan is still on the job.
I have tried to give the reasons why, in my judgment, he is not a fit and proper person for the position he holds. We have heard a good deal in this House this session about the dismissal of officials. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said that officials have been dismissed by this Government for very slight cause, and in some cases without any justification whatever. Be that as it may, I will go this far and say that I think scores of officials have lost their positions without there being against them one-hundredth part of the evidence which I have adduced here why this man should lose his position.
Another man to whom I have called attention is the hospital overseer, H. W. Wilson, who was appointed by this Government. It has been shown in the evidence-you will see it corroborated on pages 570, 571, 592 and 593 of the evidence-that he repeatedly refused to get up at night to attend to convicts who were sick and required his attention, and in some cases were even dying. The commission makes use of these very peculiar words (page 24) in regard to this matter :
Your commission are of the opinion that these patients-
That is, the ones I have spoken of as being neglected.
Your commission are of the opinion that these patients were practically beyond human aid and that in their cases no hardship was inflicted toy Wilson's failure to get up to see them; yet, we feel that the physician, or his representative, should be present on such occasions and that there should be a regulation to this effect.
Is that not a very peculiar statement for this Commission to make? In the first place they start out to justify Wilson for not getting up on the ground that these men were practically beyond aid and if he had got up to give assistance to these dying men they would have died anyway. There fore, to carry the matter to its logical conclusion, afe they were going to die anyway.

I call attention to the fact that a man who was sent to Kingston from Dorchester was hosed, notwithstanding the fact that he had been sent to Kingston as an insane convict. The inspector, as appears on page 1556 of the evidence, said that the surgeon's certificate that the man was physically fit for corporal punishment was all that he required. That may be strictly according to regulation, I have no doubt that Inspector Stewart is perfectly sincere in the belief that hosing is a most efficient and effective form of punishment. I have no quarrel with him on that point; he is entitled to liis opinion, but I most emphatically assert that I am opposed to the use of the hose on convicts, whether sane or insane. I do not believe that turning a water pressure of 60 or 75 pounds upon a man will do him any good. Perhaps I am not qualified to speak definitely in this respect, but that is my opinion. According to the evidence, page 1559, a mere boy who was sent to the institution was punished on December 12, 1911; on January 1, 12, and 13, 1912; on January 1, February 1, 22, and 24, March 15 and 26, 1913. Dr. Young said in his evidence that there was no doubt wliatever that the boy had been insane for years and was in-

sane while he was undergoing that punishment. I do not say that he was hosed, but he -was punished in various ways. He was put in the punishment cells, put on bread and water, put in the prison of isolation, put on half rations, deprived of light in his cell, suspended for 48 hours in his cell. We are all anxious to finish the business of the session, but if we were to stay here for the next six months, this is a matter that we ought to deal with, and deal with seriously, with a view to preventing the recurrence of anything of the kind in the future. Dr. Etherington declared that while the investigation was going on there were two insane convicts in the prison of isolation who should be in the insane ward. Yet the officers who, I claim, are largely responsible for this condition of affairs, still retain their positions.
There are several other matters to which I might refer, but I will not touch upon them at the present moment. It may be asserted that in my discussion of penitentiary matters, although I have been engaged in making adverse criticism, I have offered comparatively few suggestions in the way of reform. I should like hon. gentlemen to remember that I made certain specific charges; it seemed to me that I should justify the position that I took; that I should show why I believed that these men were unfit for the positions which they hold, and why I believe it is not possible to carry out any reform in the institution so long as these men are allowed to retain their positions.
I should like to make one or two suggestions with regard to prison reform. I express it as my opinion that a retrograde step was taken in the matter of prison management when the law was changed in 1875. Previous to that time the management of our prisons was under the control of a board of directors. The law was changed, and since that time they have been under practically the management of one man. I believe that a board of directors for our penal institutions should be provided. In no department, in no branch of the public service, do the officers require to possess such broad vision and sympathy, such firmness of character and temperament, such tactful kindness as is required of officers engaged in the administration of our penitentiaries. It is unreasonable, I say, to expect one person to possess all the mental and moral qualities necessary to enable him to

deal adequately with a diversified criminal population.
I would favour an indeterminate sentence. I believe that eonvicts under 21 years of age should be kept entirely separate from the older convicts, and should not be allowed to associate with them. If it is said that there is not sufficient accommodation to carry out that principle, then I say that the accommodation should be secured, and the sooner the better.
The pardoning and paroling of first offenders should be carried out in a more generous manner than it is at the present time. I am glad to see that the parole system has been advanced in this country; I think it may advantageously be extended still further. I think it is particularly worth while when applied to young convicts who are serving their first sentence.
The time involved in remission of sentences might well be reasonably extended. In California, I understand, the remission granted in each of the first two years, if the convict has conformed with regulations and has behaved himself, is two months. In each of the next two years he is allowed four months, and after that he is allowed a remission of five months in each year during the period of sentence. This remission is worth while. There is great encouragement to the convict in remissions of this kind, and the officers are enabled more efficiently to administer the prison, because the prisoners, working for these remissions, are more amenable to the rules.
Discipline must of course be maintained in any prison, but I doubt if discipline ever yet reformed a matured criminal. As a rude,' severe punishment hardens the convict and makes him more vicious and unruly, while firm kindness and tact softens, overcomes and subdues the evil in him. You may say that that is all theory, but the best test of the worth of the method is to consider whether it would be effective if applied to ourselves. Every one of us here could be led more easily than we could be driven. We would be more amenable to kindness and tact than to severe measures. In California they make food a disciplinary agent. All the food is supposed to be wholesome, but they have their tables graded; at some tables the food is better, more tasty than at other tables, and that is made use of as an inducement to convicts to obey the regulations. They also make the use of tobacco a disciplinary agent. They withhold or grant it

to the convict as his conduct warrants. I would grant tobacco to the convict in the penitentiary. I think a mistake was made when it was withdrawn from him. I believe there has been more trouble in the institution because of the withdrawal of tobacco from convicts than from any other one source.
The writing and receiving of letters might be made use of as a disciplinary agent. A convict is now allowed to communicate with his friends once in two months. That seems to be hard. Surely there is some bond of love between that convict and some one on the outside. What harm could be done by allowing him to communicate with his wife or family? It seems to me it would have a good rather than a bad effect. That privilege might be withheld or extended according as the convict obeys the rules. Lights in cells might be withdrawn as a punishment. Those are some of the means that I think would have a better and more salutory effect than putting a convict in a cell and knocking him about with a stream of water at 60 or 70 lb. pressure to the inch.
Labour is a necessity to the physical, moral and mental well-being of convicts; but if it is to be of any reformative value that labour should be productive. I do not call work on the stone pile, where a man or boy sits down month after month and year after year and pounds a larger stone into smaller particles, labour. That cannot have any good effect on the convict; on the contrary, as he smashes the stone he smashes his whole mental and moral nature, he crushes the life and ambition out of himself. It is a crying shame that, in this day, perhaps one-quarter of the convicts in Kingston penitentiary are engaged in the occupation of simply breaking stone month after month, year after year. Some men say that we cannot have productive labour in prisons because it competes with free labour. Working for the State, a convict does not augment the number of labourers in the country any more than he would if he were working outside. If he was a free man he would be in competition with the men outside. Competition, therefore, is not increased if he is inside the walls of a penitentiary. What kind of labour might be engaged in? One of our prison inspectors, Mr. Douglas Stewart, and his colleague at that time, Inspector Dawson, at one time a member of this House, made suggestions in their report to the Government in regard to prison labour which I am sorry to say
were never carried out. I firmly believe that had the suggestions which those men made at that time been carried into effect our prisons would have been far better today and some of the men who are leaving the prisons worse than when they entered would have left them better than when they entered. What did these inspectors suggest? They suggested that prison labour might be directed first, to some imported articles made in other countries and brought into Canada, second, to commodities which are temporarily or otherwise controlled by monopolies and, third, to some articles required for the use of the public service, mail bags, boots, caps and uniforms for the militia, letter carriers, customs officers and others, clothing for Indians and industrial schools, certain needs for the Northwest Mounted Police, and lighthouse service and rural nfail boxes. It seems to me that these are things that might be manufactured at our penitentiaries. I am not sure, but I would say that quite a number of our mail boxes have in the past been imported from the United States. These might have been made in the prisons. I suggested here a few years ago to the minister, and I repeat the suggestion, that one of the things that the prisoners might be employed in making is concrete tile for culverts and arches for use in road-building throughout the country. In some of the county jails throughout Ontario prisoners are employed in making tile. These are supplied to municipalities at cost. In Kingston, where they have an abundance of limestone and easy access to sand and gravel, where the cement could be shippeJ in, it seems to me that concrete arches and tiles for use in our roads could be made and handed over to the various municipalities at the actual cost of manufacture. I believe that most of the articles I have mentioned -could be made with the facilities they now have in the prison. What is the situation to-day? A prisoner now leaves prison, after putting in his sentence, without a trade, without a cent of money, broken down in health and crushed in spirit; and yet we expect that man to go out to the world and make good. What chance has he to make good and who is to blame that he has not a chance? I say we are to blame.
Hear, hear.

I would not go as far
as my hon. friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) in regard to hanging; but I do think that there are worse things even than hanging in this country. To take hoid

of a boy, to put him in the penitentiary and deprive him of any chance of ever becoming "a useful citizen, is even worse than putting a rope around his neck and hanging him. Imagine a case coming before a judge. I have in mind now a boy who came before the commission being only then between 15 and 16 years of age. He had been convicted and sentenced to Kingston for four years by a fool of a magistrate in the county of Hastings. Why? What had he done? This poor lad had been working for a farmer, he had stolen a cheap watch and $2.50 in money, and the magistrate sent that boy, between 14 and 15 years of age, down to Kingston for four years! He walked in through the gate, his name was entered, he was given a number and a suit of clothes, his hair was cut and he was shaved and washed. Then he was passed over to deputy warden, who assigned, him his work. That boy was put on the stone pile, and week after week and month after month, sat on the stone pile alongside old recidivists, old, hardened criminals. And we expect that boy at the end of four years to come out a fine type of man and to make a good citizen ! The judge might just as well say to that boy, whose moral perceptions were not hardened, who was not depraved, who was rot criminal by nature, who had made his first mistake: "Here, my boy; you are young, you are green and unsophisticated, you have taken your first step in crime, but there is a lot for you to learn before you become a graduate in criminology; so I am going to send you down to an institution where you will have all the advantages of intimate association with men who have gone through the college of crime and are past graduates in the art of committing crime; you will have an opportunity to rub shoulders with them day by day, and if there is -anything that one of them cannot tell you some of the others will; your mind is plastic and easily moulded, you are susceptible to impressions; go down there to that university of criminology where you will have an opportunity of mixing with old experienced masters in crime; you will be right alongside of them day after day, and they will teach you the various things you have to learn before you can become a graduate in crime." The judge might go on and say: " Down there you will find grades of society just as there are outside; you will find some men of the type of Travers, the man who ruined a great many people in this country by his management of the 
Farmers Bank; he has had the advantage of home training and education; you will find him eating off a plate with a knife and fork and spoon; he gets pudding and other delicacies, probably a box of cigars now and then, and occasionally a little liquor is sent him; but, of course, my boy, you are not in that class; you are only young; you have not got to the point where you can wreck hundreds of people; you have all that to learn, so we will send you where you will have an opportunity of learning it." And what happens? If the boy is sharp and has taken advantage of his association with criminals, at the end>of four years he comes out of that institution a graduate in the art of crime. He knows how to commit the greater offences against society; he has been initiated into the higher degrees of crime. He comes out a graduate of criminology and a satire on our civilization in this country. That is the condition of affairs under our penal institutions as they exist to-day.
I want to enter my protest against existing conditions. .1 say, give these convicts some productive employment. Allow them to make many of the things which we use in various branches of the service, if by so doing you can teach that lad or man a trade and bring back his self-respect. I deplore and protest against the forms of punishment in those institutions, such as the tubbing and hosing of insane convicts, and I dare say the same thing takes place in other institutions. I firmly believe, others to the contrary notwithstanding, that that form of punishment does no good to the institutions, and does irretrievable harm to the convict who is so punished.
I am aware that those who criticise my remarks will say that I have not given a very good certificate to the person from whom I have received most of the information on which my charges are based. That is very true. I have not. They may also say that I have not- given a very good certificate to the commission that held this investigation. Well, I am not at all satisfied with the way that investigation was held. I have drawn certain facts from the evidence adduced before that commission, and from other sources absolutely reliable, and I challenge any man to contradict any statement of fact which I have made tonight. I regret that the commission did not go more fully into these matters and make a more thorough investigation. Certain changes have taken place. I do not believe there has been any tubbing or hosing

lately* and I hope those forms of punishment will never be reintroduced. I hope that before this debate closes, the House and the country will have the benefit of suggestions from men on both sides of the House, many of whom I feel certain are far more capable of presenting this subject to the House than I.

I am sure we have all listened with a great deal of interest to the expose made by the hon. member for Erontenae (Mr. Edwards.) But I do not think he went far enough in telling the minister just what should be done. He has shown very conclusively that Kingston penitentiary and the other penitentiaries are a disgrace to this country, but he did not go far enough. I do not intend to delay the passing of my hon. friend's Estimates in any way. I do not want to have them reduced either, for I think they are far too small for what I am going to ask him to do. I believe I am within the mark in saying that the management of prisons and prisoners in Canada has, to say the least, been most barbarous. We are certainly committing blunders to-day that in a very short time men will point to as the most extraordinary mistakes any government could have made. Our reforms are most certainly surrounded by the most barbarous methods which the most heathenish nation has ever employed. We continue to shut up in an iron cage our poor erring brother, when we should put him to work at some useful employment in God's sunlight and in God's fresh air. The Royal Commission that the minister appointed has reported that our penitentiaries are in a deplorable condition, and certainly the condition of affairs that exists or did exist is anything but a credit to the Minister of Justice and his Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I presume the hon. gentleman has read over the evidence before venturing to make that statement?

I have read the report that has been laid on the table of the House of the commission appointed by the minister himself. The hon. member for Frontenac says they kept a great deal back, but there is sufficient in that report, I think, to make the people of this country hang their heads in shame. I regret to have to say that Kingston penitentiary has earned for itself a vary unenviable reputation as an institution for the reformation of prisoners, or for the recovery of the poor unfortunate convicts in the insane 111
ward. The minister knows that just as well as I do. I want to say to the minister that we are going about this thing wrongly, and I think he will agree with me. There was a time when the minister did not have in his heart that vengeance that he appears to have had in recent years since he came into politics. I say that the visiting of vengeance upon transgressors should no longer be tolerated in any scheme of civilized government. It is held, on the other hand, by those who have conducted the most exhaustive researches into the relations of individuals with their fellowmen, that the state has a two-fold responsibility imposed upon it; first, its duty toward its citizenship as a whole, and secondly, its duty toward the individual violator of the law. In other words, the purpose of punishment in the broadest sense is, in the first place, to protect all citizens from the menace of criminal acts, and secondly, to place such restrictions upon the transgressor as will result in his reformation and the exemplification, through such measures, of the hazardous and disastrous nature of crime.
Instead of reforming criminals the Canadian system has really been making criminals. What good does it do to hang them or to shut them up in an iron cage? If you want to see what can be done with prisoners I would invite the Minister of Justice to visit the Guelph prison farm, and there see the result of the reforms inaugurated by the Hon. Mr. Hanna, of the Ontario Government.
I think that this is one bright spot in the Dominion of Canada where an attempt has been made for the reform of prisoners. If he will look at what can be done and compare it with what is being done under the mismanagement of our prisons and prisoners, he will agree with me, that to say the least of it, the management is most brutal. It is enough to make Canadians hang their heads in shame. Does it not now become the duty of Canada to raise herself to some standard of reform, both by abolishing the death penalty and instituting reforms amongst our prisoners, or at least amongst the young and less hardened criminals. Society should be more concerned in the reformation of the man than in his punishment.
My hon. friend from Frontenac cited the case of California. I have here quite a number of reports from different states. I will give my hon. friend the Minister of Justice a few facts to show what is being



done in the state of Colorado. The Governor of Colorado, six or seven years ago, found that the penitentiary of that state was conducted on the same principles as those which seem to govern the management of our penitentiaries in Canada. He wanted to institute some reforms there and he did so. He got hold of a bright young Irishman, brought him in from the outside and appointed him warden of the Colorado penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was a good beginning.

criminals is less feared than penal servitude for life. Innocent individuals are Occasionally executed, which makes the State a murderer of the worst kind. It prevents reparation in case of subsequently proven innocence, is irrevocable, too extreme a measure; with a wrong verdict, and the sentence earried out, the mistake cannot be rectified.
4.	All punishment should be reformatory,
not vindictive. Two or more men, organized under a form of Government, have no more right to take life than one man has. It is murder in either case, and brutalizing in both.	.

There are fewer murders per capita in states and countries which have abolished the death sentence than in those states and countries who still stand for capital punishment, It deprives the criminal of the one due which civilized society owes to its unfortunate children of this class, the chance for spiritual reformation and expiation, to prepare for the hereafter.
6.	It is a relic of barbarism and of the dark and pestilential days of Nero misrule in Rome. Life imprisonment is a severer and juster punishment than the death penalty.

I submit respectfully to the ruling of the Chair, but I would like to place on record the opinion of an authority on hanging for crime. This is one of the greatest authorities that Canada has ever produced, and no one on this side of the Atlantic has ever had his experience in this matter. This is reprinted from the Maritime Baptist, and it is a conversation with Radcliffe, one of the employees of the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg pardon; he is an employee of the Provincial Government, which the hon. gentleman supports in Quebec.
I thought he must have been in the employee of the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I sometimes can stop him from hanging, but I never have authorized him hanging any one; that is done on the judgment of the provincial courts.
I think the Minister of Justice has something to do with hangings. A man said the other night that when the minister turned down his thumbs it meant no mercy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not always turn my thumbs down.

You do not always turn your thumbs down; thank God foT that. This is the conversation with Radcliffe, the late official hangman of Canada, as published in a Socialist weekly:
It appears that he was the son of an English clergyman, and during his twenty-one years as executioner he was the means of sending one hundred and thirty-souls into eternity. Referring to his first execution, that of Burchell, of Woodstock, Ont., he said the crime for which he was found guilty was so terrible " that I had no compunction about putting him out cjf business in quick manner." Very different was his story of later hangings. " My family deserted me and changed their names, but I kept right on the job because I argued with myself that, if I was doing wrong, then the Government of the country was wrong, and would be punished. I held that I was the Minister of Justice at a hanging, and that if I was a murderer, he was also a murderer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That used to be under a previous Administration, but not now.

I am glad there has been some improvement. It' has taken a long time.
And so I pacified by conscioenec in that way for many years, but of late it is killing me. The remorse which comes over me is terrible, and my nerves give out until I have not slept

for days at a time. I suffered agony of mind that was terrible, and began to feel as if iron bars tightened around me. I used to say to condemned persons, as I beckoned with my hand, " Come with me." Now at night when I lay dO'.Vn, I start with a roar as victim after victim come up before me. I can see them on the trap waiting a second before they faced their Maker. They taunt me and haunt me until I am nearly crazy with an unearthly fear. I will go to hell sure, and terrible punishment, for I am two hundred times a murderer, but I won't kill another man. I had always thought capital punishment was right, but not now. I Relieve the Almighty will visit the Christian nations with dire calamity if they don't stop taking the lives of their fellows, no matter how heinous the crime. Murderers should be allowed to live as long as possible and work out their sa'vation on behalf of the State. It is the only solution, for the stamp of Cain is on my brow, and the brow of the Government and the nation, as long as capital punishment is practised on this globe. It is a question whether a good living man could be found who would act as official hangman, and if found, whether he could be saved from demoralization. Is it expedient that one now and again should be ruined in order to the carrying out of capital punishment? Who can say the ruination is confined to one?
I regret very much that you, Mr. Chairman, would not let me go on with my reasons for asking that capital punishment should be abolished. The hon. Minister of Justice a few days ago, when the question came up before, called upon his followers to vote down the Bill which I introduced. In his argument against that measure, he made use of some of the most outrageous and startling statements that I have ever heard made in this House by a responsible minister of the Crown. He referred to the case in British Columbia, which my right hon. leader remembers, where a man was hanged because he happened to be in bad company. The Minister of Justice has suddenly developed remarkable facilities for mindreading. He told us that that man, whom he takes the full responsibility of sending into eternity-and he makes a boast of his action-had a bad heart; that he had murder in his heart. The hon. minister gave a very lengthy excuse for having senf that man to the gallows. He reads that unfortunate man's heart, and tells this House quite seriously that all the man did was to prepare himself so that,

If promise of conciseness will win the indulgence of the House, I shall have their favour while for a few moments I direct your attention to one or two matters that occur to me in reference to the subject under discussion. You will remember that in 1912 I first directed the attention of the House to the conditions as I understood them in the penitentiary at Kingston. Later on the hon. member for Frontenac again drew the attention of the House to these conditions, and, as a result of certain charges made by him, a commission was appointed to investigate, and further powers were given it as to a general investigation of the conditions of the penitentiaries of of Canada. I have listened with considerable attention and great interest to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) this eveningj, which showed .his characteristic care and which was delivered with characteristic vigour. If I might summarize his address, it would be divided into three parts. The first was a vigorous complaint against Inspector Hughes as to the character of the evidence adduced by him; the second was a eomplaint against the commission appointed by the Minister of Justice; and the third was a complaint against the penitentiary system as it exists in Canada to-day. As to the first complaint of the hon. member from Frontenac, that Inspector Hughes, then-Accountant Hughes, gave to the hon.

member certain facts and figures that were afterwards not substantiated when the commission meets. I cannot give any opinion, as I did not enjoy the confidence of the then accountant to the same degree as did the hon. member for Frontenac. However. as two members of the commission well known to me come from my riding, it is perhaps not amiss that I should differ from the hon. member for Frontenac in my conclusions as to the work of these gentlemen.
Mr. G. Mi. MacdoneM is a lawyer of some 65 or 70 years of age, a man who has given much of his life to the study of social questions, a man who enjoys the confidence of the whole community in which he lives. Dr. Etherington is a graduate of Queens' university, a fellow student of my own, a man who took a distinguished course in medicine, who walked the hospitals of Europe, came back to Kingston and has since practised successfully his profession in Kingston and district. The hon. member for Frontenac, in his speech of last year, said:
I may say that at the time the names of the commissioners were first mentioned as appointees I saw no reason why they should not perform their duties properly and well.
The hon. member for Frontenac in that expression of opinion therefore admitted that , at the time the members of the commission were appointed, he had no reason to assume that they would discharge their duty in anything but a proper manner. The hon. member for Frontenac has also quoted from the press of the country as to the conditions in the penitentiary and as to the reforms that ,members of the press think should be brought about. The late Principal Grant taught me one thing I have never forgotten. In that terse, epigrammatic way of his he said: "A man must never forget that an editorial in a paper is no greater than the man who holds the pen." I sometimes think that we are apt to attach too much importance to expressions of newspaper opinion. I appreciate the power of the press; I appreciate the tremendous weight it has in the formation of public opinion. But when we read editorial comment, we should give no greater weight to it than we would give to the expression of the individual opinion of the editor, if expressed in spoken rather than in printed words.
However, the hon. member for Frontenac has taken the liberty of quoting to this House expressions of opinion of the
[Mr. Nickle.j
Standard, of Kingston, and, therefore, since he has quoted from that paper believing it is entitled to weight, he surely will not object to my quoting from the same paper as to the character of the commissioners named by the Minister of Justice. On the 28th day of August, subsequent to the formation of the commission, the Standard, of Kingston, said as follows:
The appointment of Dr. Etherington, of this city as the third member of the commission to conduct the penitentiary investigation is an excellent one and will, we feel sure, be generally commended. This appointment completes the commission, the other members being G. M. Macdonell, K.C., chairman-an ideal man for that position-and Mr. Joseph Downey, ex-M.P.P.

The Government has made no mistake in appointing G. M. Macdonell, of this city, as chairman of the commission that is to investigate the Portsmouth penitentiary.
