These quotations are from the Conservative paper of Kingston. I now direct your attention to a quotation from the British Whig, a Liberal organ, dated a few days after August 28. This paper said:
The Whig is under no obligation to defend these men politically, as they owed their choice, primarily, to the fact that they were good Conservatives. But they possessed, apart from their political calling, special qualifications for the work. Mr. Macdonell, the chairman, had for many years given penology a very close study. He was largely interested in the reform of erring humanity. Dr. Etherington was chosen, it is presumed, because of his professional training, and because one very distinct phase of the inquiry was of a man of unbiased mind. Mr. Downey was, in a sense, a specialist in the service to which he was called in this case.
Mr. Downey, as you know, was a member of the commission appointed by Hon. Mr. Hanna to inquire into the American system of penitentiaries and reformatories, and it was through the report of that commission that the Guelph institution came into existence. So much for the personnel of the commission. Perhaps I should say, in passing, that I think possibly it was unfortunate that the powers of the commission included the investigation of the charges of the hon. member for Frontenac and also an inquiry into general penitentiary conditions. At the time the commission was launched the

member for Frontenac readily admits that he was primarily concerned with the investigation of the personal charges against the men of whom he made complaints, and that he suffered annoyance when his chief witness, Accountant Hughes, did not come forward with evidence of the state of facts, as he had hoped he would. The net result was that very soon the commission and the hon. member for Frontenac came to grips, and there were several lively sittings, if one may judge from the report in the daily papers throughout the country.
I had not the privilege, or rather I did not take advantage of my opportunity, of attending the commission, and therefore as to what took place I must speak purely from hearsay; but I am satisfied that if the commission came to tan erroneous conclusion as to the weight to be attached to the evidence given before them, that conclusion was an erroneous conclusion honestly reached. Thera was no such thing as what the hon. member for Frontenac calls " deliberate misrepresentation." In support of the statement that the members of the commission were characterized by deliberate misrepresentation, the hon member for Frontenac draws the attention of the House to the fact that in the commission's report they make reference to certain paging in the evidence, but do not give a reference to those pages. I think if the hon. member for Frontenac had stopped for a moment to consider the matter he would have readily seen that the report of the commission, as submitted to the Minister of Justice, would necessarily be typewritten or written in longhand and the evidence given before the commission *would be in typewritten form. In other words, if the commission in their report had placed the number of the pages in the report it would not be the same number of page if the evidence had been printed. The commission at the time they submitted their report were not in a position to know whether or not the evidence would be printed. They knew the evidence would be offered to the Minister of Tustice, hut they could not know whether or -not that evidence would come in a printed form to the House. They therefore did what any lawyer, what any member of a commission would naturally do:	they left the page
blank but made a reference to tne paging with the intent probably that that paging would be put in by whomsoever had the report printed and submitted for distribution. The hon. member for Frontenac draw's attention to the fact-
Could they not have referred to the page of the typewritten evidence?

My hon. friend from Frontenac asks me if that could not have been done as well if the page of the typewritten evidence had been put in. It would have been most misleading if the evidence had been printed. The printed pages would have been totally different from the typewritten pages. The documents of the future would have referred to the typewritten reports, and confusion would inevitably have resulted.
If they had the typewritten documents printed, how would they know to what page the commission referred?

It certainly shows no deliberate intention to deceive on the part of the commission.
The hon. member for Frontenac has drawn the attention of the House to the case of Gliartrand, a convict who escaped. He has said that Chartrand's case showed the intention of the commission to misrepresent, because they did not come to a conclusion in regard to the matter nor adequately report to the Minister of Justice, i should like the members of the House who happen to have in their hands the report of that commission to turn their attention to page 22, charge (e):
Charge (e) :	That the deputy was guilty of
gross neglect of duty resulting in attempts to escape.
The particular case cited was that of Chartrand, a convict, who cut through the bars of his cell and got into the yard of the prison, and the charge is that an inexperienced guard and inefficient guard had been placed in supervision of this convict. This case was fully investigated at the time by the minister, and Guards Smith and McConville were suspended for their conduct in the matter.
And there is much more with which I v ill not weary the House. There was an inquiry before the Minister of Justice covering some 30 pages. The minister gave judgment, and this is the last clause of the inquiry referred to on page 23 of this report :
The minister's judgment reflects on "the insufficiency of the right surveillance provided " and " concurs in the suggestion " that the warden and deputy warden be censured for neglect to profit by the attempted escape from an adjoining cell last year," etc., etc. There is no suggestion of such censure in the inspector's report, it does not appear in the record, so that we are unable to attach to it the correct significance, but considering that this whole matter was fully dealt with and adjudicated on by the minister at the time of this occurrence, it should

not again be made the subject of a charge before this commission. In any case, the whole record is on file and can be referred to, if, in the opinion of the minister, the matter should be reopened.
That makes it amply clear in that one particular case to which the hon. member for Frontenac has directed the attention of the House, the commission placed the matter before the Minister of Justice for consideration because he had the evidence iu his possession. It is not my intention to follow the hon. member for Frontenac through the numerous cases cited
by	him	from	the evidence. I havenot	had	the	pleasure of seeing acopy	of	the	evidence, and those
of us whose duty it has been through life to value evidence know how easily it is to pick out evidence here and there and make a tolerably well-founded argument. I am not going the length of saying that the hon. member for Frontenac is not correct in his conclusions, but I say that he loses sight of a great opportunity for good when in his zeal to secure the dismissal of two men-and the hon. gentleman to-night has made out a strong case for their dismissal -he blinds himself to the importance of this report. That this commission did not intend to cover up or shield anybody is seen from the fact that they reported in regard to the present physician in a way altogether beyond the charges made by the hon. member for Frontenac. Take, for instance, page 12 of their report in regard to the condition of the insane wards. No charge was made by the hon. member for Frontenac as to the condition of the insane patients, but this is what the commission says:
It being generally' agreed that the condition of the Insane is and has been for years altogether unsatisfactory, the question "who are responsible? " demands an answer. The responsibility falls primarily upon two men, the surgeon and the inspector. The former, in his annual reports, should have given expression to views [DOT] such as he presented in his evidence before the commission. This was clearly his duty and would have relieved him of responsibility, but unfortunately a perusal of his reports leaves one with the impression that the state of the insane left nothing to be desired.
Could there be a more drastic criticism of the surgeon than that? Turn to the hospital in regard to which the surgeon was responsible:
The operating room (so-called), where serious cases have been, and must be dealt with as they arise, has an old wooden table but no other equipment. When your commissioners visited this room, many old books lay about the floor and the place was not clean. In all, there was a

condition of affairs which should not have been tolerated. Again, there is to be noted an all hut complete absence of satisfactory records. Inspector Stewart's commendation of the existing conditions can only mean that he is not competent to express an opinion upon this aspect of prison management. Although his annual reports give a different impression, the surgeon in his evidence before the commission stated that many changes were necessary to make the hospital what it should be. . . .
We have no hesitation in reaching the following conclusions:
The hospital, in building, equipment, and sanitation is inadequate and out of date, and the personnel is not adapted to proper hospital administration.
There should be provided a new hospital, modern in plan and equipment, and the hospital staff should be reorganized, the members to consist of:	A visiting surgeon, a resident
physician, two trained male nurses, and convict orderlies.
Could there be a more drastic criticism of the surgeon than that? I cite these instances only to show to the House that it was the intention of the commission to shield nobody. They evidently felt the evidence in regard to specinc charges was not sufficiently strong to warrant conclusions that may have been in accord with the wishes and intent of the hon. member for Frontenac. That was probably the conclusion of the commission. But this shows clearly that the intention of the commission was not to shield but rather to lay bare to the public view the existence of facts as they found them at the Kingston penitentiary.
What were the reommen'dations of the penitentiary commission? I should like these to go on Hansard for the guidance of future members of Parliament:
Recommendations.
Your commissioners beg to make the following recommendations:
Management.
(1)	That the control of the penitentiaries be placed in the hands of a permanent commission of three members, with power to appoint staff officers and heads of departments, make regulations for the government of the institutions and generally direct their management.
(2)	That under such commission the warden of each prison be given full authority to employ and-dismiss'keepers, guards, etc., in addition to the powers he now enjoys.
(3)	That a Parole Board of not less than three members be appointed for each penitentiary. to sit once a month and to hear and consider applications for parole, and make recommendations on the same to the Minister of Justice.
(4)	That the field staff of the parole organization be increased to three officers to be directly under the charge of the Department of Justice and work in conjunction with the local parole boards.

Classification.
(5)	That an arrangement be entered into with the provinces of the Dominion to take over the custody of first offenders and prisoners under twenty-five years of age.
(6)	That should it be found impracticable to carry out recommendation No. 5, two reformatories for young prisoners and first offenders be established-one in the East and the other in the West.
< 7) That within the present penitentiaries a system of classification be inaugurated, based upon the conduct of the prisoners, and operated with a view to encourage them to habits or order, industry, and a better appreciation of the duties of citizenship.
Industrial Employment.
(8)	That what is known as the State-use or Public-use system of prison labour be adopted throughout the penitentiaries and that industries be established to supply the requirements of the Government, its institutions and services, with all goods that can be made in prison.
(9)	That outside labour be developed to the fullest possible extent at each prison, in farming operations and, where raw material can be conveniently obtained, in quarrying stone, making brick, etc.
Treatment of Prisoners.
(10)	That a thorough physical and mental examination be made of each prisoner on his admission, and as far as possible his antecedents and family history be obtained and put on record; and
That a proper filing system be installed at each penitentiary, so that the history, physical and mental condition of the prisoner on admission and his record in prison may be kept in one envelope.
(11)	That the close cropping of prisoners' hair be abolished, except in cases where it is necessary to preserve cleanliness.
(12)	That in place of the present prison uniform a suit and cap of one tone material, blue or grey, be adopted.
(13)	That a few copies of a carefully censored weekly newspaper be provided in each prison for the use of good-conduct prisoners.
(14)	That a moderate issue of tobacco oe made to good conduct prisoners who had contracted the habit before entering prison.
(15)	That as soon as space can be provided a dining-room equipped with proper service be established at each prison for all good conduct prisoners, and that meanwhile the tinware utensils in use be discarded and enamel-ware substituted.
(16)	That hosing of convicts and confining them in a dark cell or dungeon and shackling with ball and chain be abolished.
The Hospital and Insane Ward.
(17)	That a hospital, modern in plan and equipment, he provided.
(IS) That, the hospital staff be reorganized so that it comprise a visiting surgeon, a resident physician, and two trained male nurses.
(19)	That a separate institution for the criminal insane be established or that arrangements be made with the Provincial Governments for taking over this class.
The School.
(20)	That a school of letters be established te ea-h prison, and for three hours at least each
day instruction be given by a head teacher and inmate monitors.
(21)	That drill exeroises be held every Saturday afternoon when the weather is suitable, and on the afternoon of every holiday; and that an occasional entertainment be given.
Disciplinary Officers.
(22)	That in the employment of guards more regard be had to the charaoter and education of the applicant, with a view that the official should exercise the best possible influence over the prisoner.
Indeterminate Sentence.
(23)	That the Criminal Code be so amended as to empower judges to impose a maximum and minimum term of sentence on all persons committed to a penitentiary, the period of detention to be fixed by the Parole Board.
May I ask you if that strikes you as a report of a commission which was unable to correctly size up existing conditions, or the report of a commission that had not the interest of our criminal population at heart? It strikes me entirely the other way; it strikes me as the report of a commission which desired to be thorough, which gave to the subject the best that was in them. If, in their conclusions,- and there are conclusions and recommendations in this report that would not meet with my approval-if I say, in their conclusions, they err let us at least give them the credit of being honest in what they did and in what they said and of being desirous that the best possible results might come from their inquiry. We are all expressing our views in regard to penitentiary administration and I suppose that one man's' opinion is just as much good as that of another. Somebody has said that every man who rides down the hill to the penitentiary in a motor car thinks himself competent to express an opinion as to how that penitentiary should he managed. I have done more than ride down hill in a motor car to the Kingston penitentiary; I have been through that penitentiary time and again and there has never been a time that I have gone through that my heart is not stirred with pity at the scenes I have there witnessed and I have always felt that it is worth while trying to save any man no matter how degraded he may be.
I sincerely 'doubt if we are going about it in the right way under our present penitentiary- .system. I think that my hon. friend from Frontenac is perhaps right in this, that the system is wrong and that before things are going to be better you will have to get a different system. I do not believe you can run a penitentiary system over a long distance telephone. I

do not believe you will get the right sort of man as warden of the penitentiary so long as he is subservient to a central authority. If you are going to better penitentiary conditions in this country you will have to get a big man to take the position of warden, a man who will be master of the job, who will realize the importance of the work and who will realize that if he cannot do things as they should be done the job is not worth having and who. rather than 'do things that he does not believe to be right, will vacate his position and give up the work to some one else. You cannot run a penitentiary system in my judgment by having a central inspecting bureau dictating to and controlling your warden. Under such a system as that you develop a condition of apathy, indifference, and a desire to work along the lines of least resistance rather than ia desire to improve and better the conditions of the penitentiary.
In regard to work, it is the easiest thing in the world to say that work should be provided for convicts. Inspector Stewart, in report after report, has recommended that work be found. It is a difficult thing to find work for convicts in this country. In summer time it is easy enough to buy a few hundred acres of land and, if you have sufficient guards, to put these men out on the land. But you have long winter months and for six or seven months in the year it is impossible to develop along agricultural lines and the men must necessarily do their work inside. What work are they going to do? It certainly is unfair that convict labour should be brought into conflict with free labour. Free labour has the right to get the product of its toil and that product must not be undersold by the product of the penitentiary. If you are not going to bring the labour of the penitentiary into conflict with free labour how are you going to work out the scheme? I am inclined to think that possibly my hon. friend from Frontenac is right in saying that you should allow the penitentiaries to supply the State's needs. It has been done in the state of New York and I believe that the labour interests of the country are big enough and broad enough to realize that just because a man has made one, or possibly two slips, that does not put him outside the universal brotherhood of man or that therefore some arrangement should not be made by which penitentiary labour could be productively employed.
I agree with my hon. friend from
fMr. Niekle.]
Frontenac that the stone pile iniquity should not be tolerated for another hour. To see men and boys, hour after hour and day after day, pounding away on that stone pile is something that cannot fail to arouse sympathy. No sooner is one load of stone carted away than another is brought in. It reminds me of one of the mythological tales, according to which a man had to roll two stones to the top of the hill, and his punishment was complete when both reached the top. When he got one stone the whole way up, for some unaccountable reason the hill shook and the stone rolled to the bottom. There is nothing original about this work, there is nothing productive, there is nothing to stimulate ambition; and after a man has broken stone for a long time he has broken his soul, and his spirit and ambition have left him.
Take the question of the children that are in the penitentiary. My hon. friend from Frontenac has stated that ten per cent of the population of the penitentiary is under 20 years of age. I have seen children in our penitentiaries 16, 17 and even 13 years of age-I am not so sure about 13 years of age-sent there by irresponsible magistrates and judges, and yet I have heard it stated that these children, who could neither read nor write, should not have the privilege of a simple education because, forsooth, we might be educating criminals. I would like to ask the man who advocates that doctrine if it is not better to believe that, instead of educating a criminal, you might be making an honest man? If we are going to have children put in our penitentiaries, let us make some arrangement by which they can get a reasonable education; let us turn them out into the world with the rudiments of an education, so that when they come to fight their own battle of life, they may have the accomplishments of the common school, and not be ignorant of the simpler things of life.
I am glad to say that the insane problem, I believe, has been solved. I understand that arrangements have been made with the provinces by which the insane population of Kingston penitentiary is to be taken charge of by the various provinces temporarily. That is a move in the right direction. It recognizes that insanity is a disease, and that the insane are capable of being treated in such a way as to bring about improvement. It is not nec*sr \ry revert to the soul-harrowing conditions which existed in the insane ward at Kingston. These conditions are gone. My hon. friew itom Frontenac deserves

credit, and it must be a gratification to him to know that at least this amelioration has been brought about in the condition of this unfortunate class of people.
As to suits, cropping the hair, and all those things, I do not know whether they amount to much or not. But some great uoIdler has well said that if, during a campaign, you allow your soldiers to be unshaven and unkempt the army soon Becomes a rabble, and the rabble, a mob. I suppose the philosophy of that remark lies in this, that if you want to make a man self-respecting, you must make him tidy and feel that he is a man. One thing that struck me in the penitentiary was the garb of the convicts. What is the sense of insisting upon such a garb? The whole thing lacks, may I say, tone. It is slovenly in its detail and degrading in its colour. If we must have a distinctive garb, let us have one that will fit the man well. Let it be cut in such a way that he feels that he is still a man, and let the colour not be such as to offend his eye. It seems to be a little thing, but these are the little things that enter into the life of the convict. Let him remember the higher and bigger things in life, and do not insist upon these little things that serve only to degrade his manhood.
I had a request from a boy, who had been an accountant in a bank and who had made his first slip, and who was really heartbroken because he could write home to his mother but once in two months. What possible harm could there be in that boy writing home and benefiting by the home influence? You may say: We must have discipline. That is true, but surely the influence of home is worth something in the development of the youth.
Why all these cast-iron regulations? Discipline there must be, but let there be discretion with the warden, and if there is discretion in the warden, I believe there will be an improvement in the condition of the convicts.
As I said in the beginning, I am not going to criticise the remarks of the hon. member for Frontenae (Mr. Edwards) as to the correctness of his deductions from the evidence. I am not in a position to do so, because I have not had the evidence before me. But I do believe these commissioners were actuated by honest motives. I do believe that much good will come from their work. I think that the hon. member for Frontenae has sown the seeds of big things, and if we can develop some system by which hope will be stimulated in the minds of the men
who pass through our penitentiaries, and by which they will leave these institutions with the idea that better things are in store for them, the hon. member for Fron-tenac will have done a great work.
In Montreal the other day the Solicitor General made the statement that since 1899, 6,540 prisoners had been released from the penitentiaries on parole; that only 192 of these were convicted of crimes within the period of their parole, or 2-9 per cent of the total; that 226 violated their parole and had to be returned to the prisons, or 3J per cent; and that the total number who did not make good was 418, or only about 6 per cent. If 94 per cent of the men who are released on parole make good, why should not more of the men make good who serve out their sentences, provided they have a reasonable chance? I agree with the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Clark) who said that men should be let loose from the penitentiaries with hardened muscles and with bronzed skin, with the consciousness that they Lave another chance which it is worth while to take advantage of, and with the feeling that during their period of incarceration they have not been oppressed and down-trodden-I was going to say tortured, but I will omit that word.
. If you eliminate from a man the last sign of manhood while he is in a penitentiary, there is little chance that when he is released he will feel it worth while to try and win back in society the place which he lost.

Like other hon. members in the House, I appreciate the flow of language of my hon. friend (Mr. Nickle) and his ability tb argue on one side of a question on general principles, and on the other side of it on specific instances. The hon. member has once again repeated what he said last session, and he has intimated that in my anxiety to see a couple of officials removed from their offices I lost sight of the greater opportunity. That, of course, was intended to draw to the attention of the House what he considered my narrowness of view, and to give evidence that he was still possessed of that breadth of view which characterized him a year ago. Let me say that I do not care a snap of my finger who is deputy warden, or warden, or surgeon, or an employee of any kind in Kingston penitentiary, or in any other penitentiary. If any of these officials, on my charges, were to be removed from office, I have no persons to nominate

to take their places, and I have no intention of nominating any one. I have given what I consider good reasons why these men are unfit for their positions, and if these reasons do not appeal to the Minister of Justice, very well: he has the say in that matter, not I. If also the hon. membei for Kingston cannot see the evidence as I do, he has, of course, a right to his own view.
I said I knew nothing about it.

The hon. gentleman says he knows nothing about it, but that is not my fault. He had numerous conferences, some twenty-two or twenty-three, with the chairman of the commission while the investigation was being held, with regard to matters connected with the commission, evidence and otherwise, and I can readily understand his position here to-night with regard to the members of that commission, for I think that probably I. am right in saying that they were recommended by himself. They are at all events constituents of his,and if I cannot agree with him in regard to their handling of this matter, we will simply have to differ. The hon. member rather found fault with me for quoting so extensively from. the newspapers, and he said that it was possible we might attach too much importance to the press. Well, he gave the same quotations as he did a year ago, from the Kingston Standard and the Kingston Whig to justify himself. I also read a quotation from the Standard, and as my quotation from the Standard was of a later date than the one the hon. gentleman quoted, 1 might argue that it indicated that a change of opinion had come over the Standard as well as over myself in regard to the capability of these commissioners.
The hon. gentleman lost sight of my argument re McConville and Smith. My point and my sole point on this was that in appointing as guards men like Smith and McConville, one of whom had been reprimanded fourteen times within a few months far neglect of duty or for performing his duty inefficiently, and the other of whom had been suspended for being drunk, the deputy warden did not show good judgment. That is my view and my argument, and that argument the hon. member lost sight of entirely.
It may be that I have lost sight of a great opportunity, and that my hon. friend has been more happy than I in being able to see a great opportunity for reform. I contended, and I gave reasons for my conten-

tion, that in order to effect reform it was necessary to change some of the officials who, in my judgment, had proven themselves decidedly inefficient. I am sorry if my hon. friend and the minister cannot agree with me in that. It seems to me that I gave facts enough to 'show that these men were corrupting that institution, and 1 might quote from the words which Shakespeare puts in the mouth of Brutus:
The name of Cassius honours this corruption,
And chastisement doth therefore hide his head.
I would like to have the eloquence of my hon. friend to picture the conditions as they are in that institution. I venture to say that had he made the charges and the deductions from the evidence on which I sought my substantiation of these charges, he would have made a case very much stronger than I did, because of fiis exceptional ability not only as a speaker, but as a lawyer. However, he has not chosen to regard that side of the case at all. He contents himself with saying he did not look over the evidence. He says that the matter is one of great importance, wonderful importance. If it is of so great importance, and I do not dispute that it is, it is strange that it is not of sufficient importance for him to have given the evidence his attention. Might the hon. gentleman not have given the evidence some of his very valuable attention, in order that he might have drawn correct conclusions? I may not be able to deduce the facts from the evidence so accurately as he can, but I have at least looked the evidence over carefully and I have used what brains I have in trying to come to a proper conclusion. The hon. gentleman has placed his views before the House and has given us the benefit of his wisdom without having looked over the evidence.
So far as the commission is concerned, I -can repeat, if necessary, what I said this evening. The men on that commission lost a great opportunity; they showed again and again throughout the investigation that they were determined, so far as it lay in their power, to prevent evidence from coming up which would reveal those prison officials in their proper light. I can give dozens of cases to show that they misrepresented the evidence. They misrepresented Greer's evidence beyond the shadow of a doubt. I gave the page of the evidence, and any hon. member can consider for himself whether or not they properly represented

that evidence. For instance, on page 19, the commissioners say that the charges made refer to the present state of management of the penitentiary. That is a misrepresentation. The charges do not represent anything of the kind. The charges are there to speak for themselves. As to whether they went back of the present time is another matter. The commissioners said that the charges referred to the present time, when it was quite clear that some of the charges "went back several years. Some of those charges were shut off, because they went back of the present time.
In regard to the question of testifying falsely, the commissioners say on page 19, that that matter was considered; that it was under investigation before. That matter was never under investigation. That is a misrepresentation on their part again. Here is another one. Montgomery complained, they said, because his post was not changed as often as were those of others. Montgomery said that he resigned his position as guard because of unfair treatment by the deputy. Therefore that is a misrepresentation on their part. When such things as that appear on page after page of the report, am I not justified in saying that the commission deliberately misrepresented the evidence brought before them? If they did not deliberately misrepresent it, then why did they make statements which were at variance with the facts?
I do not know that it is necessary or advisable to argue the matter as to the personnel of the commission. The hon. member for Kingston has one view; I have a view which does not accord with his. He says that the system is wrong. I agree with that view. I say that the best system ever devised qannot be a success in the hands of men who have proved themselves as inefficient as those men have.
It is not fair to me for my hon. friend to represent me as being actuated solely along the line of the charges that I have made. I have made certain charges. If I have not justified myself in making them, I am in the judgment of the House in regard to that. But I repeat now, what I have said before and what I think my hon. friend should at least give me credit for, that my object is and has been to reform and improve conditions in our penitentiaries. The matter of the officials is of very secondary importance. The important matter is the changing of the conditions. I am honest in my belief that those conditions cannot be changed under such men as the
present officials. The main point is to effect those changes. I would be taking a very illogical position if I advocated here change and reform in our present conditions under the management of under-officers who, I fully and honestly believe	have	demonstrated their absolute inefficiency for the positions which they hold.	Whether I have made
myself clear to my hon.' friend the member for Kingston or not, I hope that I have made my position clear to the rest of the House. Last year he thought that I was holding a cent so close to my eye that I could not see the light of the sun. The hon. member for Kingston is not the only man who can see farther than the end of his nose. He is a very clever man, of course, but he must not allocate to himself all the knowledge and a-11 the breadth of vision in this country. I can hardly allow my hon. friend to do that. He has given lessons to members of this House, even to the Prime Minister; and he may feel, because he has done so and has got away with it, that small fish like myself do not count for very much. I may not; but if any imputation is thrown at me, I am going to fight back whether I am successful or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I regret very much to
delay the passing of the Estimates; but at the same time I presume it is due, if not to myself-after the description of myself which the hon. member for St. Lawrence gave, I feel that there is not very much due to myself-to the hon. members who spoke and to the importance of the subjects with which they dealt, that I should make some answer and give some expression of my own view's as to the matters that have been dealt with.
There is no possible question about the importance of our making every possible improvement in the method of dealing with out criminals. That is a very good cause, and I want to express my appreciation of everything that each of the members has said in support of that cause. I might perhaps take the liberty of pointing out that strong language does not always help the cause in which it is invoked, and that exaggeration of statement positively hurts any cause in support of which it is invoked. When the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike), for instance, described me as going about with the brand of Cain upon my brow, I do not know that it convinced any one that capital punishment ought to ne abolished.
I beg the hon minister's pardon. I did not say anything of the kind. I said that was the statement made by one of my hon. friend's own employees, Mr. Radcliffe.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When he quotes my
employee, who by the way was not my employee, I do not think that aids him to convince people that capital punishment ought to be abolished; nor do I think that the numerous strong expressions, which the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) quoted from a number of newspapers as regards the conditions existing in our penal institutions, add very much to the weight of any argument in support of the improvement of those conditions. He must remember that the newspapers must have had their information from what took place in the course of the investigation, or if not from that source, from what was said by other persons to be the result of that investigation. That being true, the fact that one newspaper, or another newspaper, described conditions as barbarous, disgraceful, indefensible, and so on, is absolutely nothing as statement of fact. That is the expression of these newspapers; we have not the advantage of knowing what was the evidence upon which they based those statements, save in so far as we may assume that they based them on the evidence taken before the commission of investigation-and that sends us right back to where we were before the newspapers talked about it.
I sympathize with the idea of doing as much to treat every convict with such humanity as is consistent with his being detained at all. I go as far as anybody can go in the desire to see convicts treated with humanity, -but when you are trying to treat the convict with humanity you must be careful, in your zeal, not to be unjust to those who occupy the position of being charged with the carrying out of the law, such as the law is, and with the administration of a system for the carrying out of that law which is prescribed by regulations made by proper authority. The hon. member for Frontenac very truly pointed out the unreliable nature of evidence which you are likely to get in investigations of this kind, by reason of the desire which the convict or the subordinate employee may have to avoid in incurring the displeasure of those who occupy positions of authority over him. I think, too, that you have to recognize the essential unreliability of the evidence of a concur. Doherty.]
vict when directed against those whose position calls upon them to exercise authority over the convict, and who may have been called upon by existing regulations to exercise even an undue severity over that convict. In investigations of this kind you are necessarily face to face with testimony of a character which calls for the very closest scrutiny, both for the reasons pointed out by the hon. member for Frontenac, and for the reasons which I have just stated. I say that because I wish to add that from that results the absolute unsafety of taking every statement that is made by one or more witnesses placed in that position-witnesses whose testimony has to be weighed in view of the existing conditions-and say that it is true. We all know that evidence has to be weighed. We all know that one man's statement is not necessarily true, even when he believes it to be true. We all know that the statement of half a dozen men, contradicted by one man, may be an untrue statement, and that the one man may be telling the truth. Everybody whose calling in life puts upon him the duty of learning something about the appreciation of evidence, first learns the absolutely elementary principle that you must weigh evidence aud not count witnesses. I can quite understand that in the position in which the hon. member for Frontenac found himself, as he described it to us this evening, he was in perfect good faith when he brought these charges, and I do not question his good faith to-night, when he re-asserted his belief in these charges. But there is only one way by which matters of this kind can be dealt with and determined. You must find a tribunal to decide when people differ about questions of this kind, and such a tribunal must necessarily decide in the one sense or in the other. It is not to be expected that the decision of such a tribunal will always carry conviction to the party against whom the finding is made, but those who are called upon to take action in consequence of the existence of a certain state of facts must be allowed to rely upon the determination of a tribunal of some kind and to govern themselves accordingly. That is the situation in which we are placed with regard to the action that ought to be taken as the result of the investigation that has been had. I am satisfied that all of us have but one common feeling in the desire to make the condition of the convict as tolerable as is consistent with the purposes for which he is detained. I think that even the

hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal, who has such a growing conviction of the hardness of my own heart, scarcely believes all the very forcible things which he said this evening with regard to my attitude upon this question. I do not know whether I shall be able to persuade him in that regard, but I know myself what my feeling is respecting the treatment of the convict, and I am satisfied that we are all agreed on that point. It is an unfortunate and much-to-be-regretted circumstance that this matter of - general interest with which we are called upon to deal should find itself bound up with a question of charges against particular individuals. In saying that, I am not minimizing the importance of what the hon. member for Frontenac says when he points out that you cannot expect the best of systems to be worked to good results if you have not good men to work it out. Certainly, if I had to choose between the two, I think I should be disposed to prefer a bad system in the hands of good men to a good system in the hands of bad men. That does not alter the fact that it is regrettable that we have to treat these matters as connected; but the situation is such that we have to do it. I have the responsibility for the method in which this was done, and I am free to admit that possibly it would have been wiser to have separated the two things absolutely; to have investigated by one commission the charges which the hon. member for Frontenac brought forward against the two officers of the penitentiary Dr. Phelan and Mr. O'Leary, and to have left the general question of penitentiary administration and conditions to be separately considered by another commission. Possibly I was unwise in that regard.

Was not the object of
appointing the commission not only to inquire into the charges which I made, but also to inquire intelligently into matters in general?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.

As the hon. minister
clearly sets forth in his commission, the commission was to investigate and report, final judgment in regard to the officials as well as in regard to the general question of administration to rest not with the tribunal, but with the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No doubt the final decision and the final responsibility rests not 112
with the tribunal, but with the department. For the moment I was pointing out that possibly it would have been wiser to separate the two things. The present remark of the hon gentleman is perhaps more applicable to something I said a moment ago about the necessity of these matters being determined by somebody. I am not seeking to shirk the responsibility of the decision that has to be made both as to the charges and as to the action that has to be taken. I would base what I say on this: We must have a method of reaching some finality upon this subject. What is the method which was adopted, a method which I think the hon. member himself would concede was a proper method. I think the hon. member will recollect that his own suggestion was that we should appoint a commission to inquire, and, as he says, to report. We selected a Commission. If ever I tried to be careful to find an impartial commission and one with regard to whom there would be the impossibility even of suggesting that I had selected the members of the commission because I was looking for a result in one direction or another, I did it that time. Everybody was agreed, I think the hon. member for Frontenac was quite agreed, when those gentlemen were appointed, that I had sucfceeded in finding an impartial commission.
I did not know anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will stand corrected if my memory deceives me, but I understood the hon. member for Frontenac, when this matter was discussed last year, to say, that at the time these names were announced as the commissioners chosen he had no fault to find.
%
That is not quite correct, that I saw no reason why they could not perform the duties properly. I candidly admit that I said that, and I am free also to say that I decidedly have changed my opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think we all quite realize that. What I wanted to point out was that I at least had got this far on a common road with the hon. member for Frontenac that I, from the best information I could get, believed I had got a perfectly impartial tribunal and he saw no reason why they should not perfectly carry out their duties.



Now, where is the parting of the ways? The parting of the ways between the hon. member for Frontenac and myself is upon the conclusion that the commission came to. His charge of opinion rests upon -the conclusion that the commission reached and the method in which he considered, in view of -the evidence, they reached that conclusion. So that we start with a commission, with no evidence to lead us to suspect the report of the commission, save the report itself. The hon. member for Frontenac discussed this commission last year and discussed this report. He discussed it on general lines, and he discussed it also with regard to the particular charges that were made against these two men. I said then that I would go into the evidence and compare it with the report, with regard more particularly to these two particular matters. I have tried to do that, putting into it the best capacity I had, and perhaps I may venture to claim that I have had some experience in the weighing of evidence. The result of my reading of the evidence, and my confronting of it with the report of the commission, I think it is only due to justice to say, is that, in so far as the charges against Mr. O'Leary are concerned, I can find no ground upon which I could disagree with the report. I am not saying, and no man can say, that the charges which the hon. member for Frontenac made were not true. But all of these matters have got to be judged on the evidence that is made. The member for Frontenac, I take it, had very much stronger grounds to believe these things to be true than he himself thinks that the evidence actually constituted. I have looked at that evidence, as I have said; I have compared it with the report, and I would be lacking in the courage to do justice if I did hot say that the results of the exercise of the best judgment that I have been able to bring to bear upon that question is that the report, in so far as it finds the charges made against Mr. O'Leary were not true, is justified by the evidence that was made before the commission. I make no profession to infallibility in that regard, but I have the responsibility, as the hon. member has pointed out, of reaching a conclusion as to the correctness of that report, and I am satisfied, as I have said, that that report is in that respect correct; and I feel, as I said at the outset, that, great as is my desire and great as should be the desire of everybody to treat with humanity and consideration the convict that has -erred, there i-s an imperative duty 
to do justice to the man against whom an offence is not established.
As regards the other charges, the charges against Dr. Phelan, you have got to divide the report which these gentlemen made between their report on the specific charges which were made and their general report upon conditions in the penitentiary that were not covered by the charges that were made.
I should say, perhaps, before I pass from thi-s, a word upon the five years limit. I may say at once that the five years limit was not intended by me, nor do the words of the commission that I issued, nor do I think the words of that commission as interpreted by the commissioners themselves, involve any limitation of five years in so far as regards any particular matter. I may cite the words:
Provided that the inquiries under paragraphs (a) and (b).
That is the management of the penitentiary and the conduct of the officers:
Shall not extend back over a longer period than five years, except in so far as the commissioners may deem it desirable, in the public interest, to inquire into any particular matter or matters antecedent to such period.
I would like to point out the condition which I found. Particular charges were made against these two men by the hon. member for Frontenac. They were addressed to me, and he asked for a commission. I acknowledged that letter, and I pointed out to the hon. member that it appeared to me that if these charges as they stood were to be submitted to a commission it would be a fair thing to communicate them to the people charged in order that an answer might be made and the issue might go to the commission. The hon. member for Frontenac answered me and said he thought it would be more desirable if a commission were appointed, and then he would lay the charges before them. I acquiesced in that manner of dealing with it. Speaking from memory, I am not quite certain whether the hon. member for Frontenac suggested to me a wider scope of inquiry or not, quite possibly it was so. I know that such suggestions were made to me by different members when the question arose, and I may say it was an idea that I *had in my own mind that it would be well to make a general inquiry and also to deal with particular matters. That general inquiry was of no interest save to enable me to judge of existing conditions, and certainly I think it would have been an unwise

thing to appoint a commission to investigate back to the time when the penitentiaries were started to ascertain how men who are dead and gone might have conducted themselves or what evils might have existed in the past. I was particularly careful to remove from them any restrictions so far as any particular matter was concerned which they might deem it desirable in the public interest to inquire into.
I presume the minister has looked at the evidence, and must have seen that the time clause was invoked again and again by the commission and by the counsel acting for the persons charged.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have seen places
where the five-year limit was combined, with other considerations. I am not prepared to say that in 2,000 pages of evidence there is no case where exclusively upon the ground of the five-year limit something has not been excluded. But 1 think that while there may have been references to the five-year limit, there were also other considerations stated as justifying the refusal to go into the inquiry of some particular matter. For instance, the charge of perjury against O'Leary. To proceed to try a man on a charge of perjury fifteen years after the alleged offence, when persons who may have been thoroughly competent witnesses at the time have disappeared or died,-I appeal to the sense of fairness of my hon. friend whether that would be a fair thing to do.
I would appeal to the sense of fairness of the minister and ask him if he made that suggestion to me at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: 1 do not recollect that the charges specified a date at all.
The charge referred to a former investigation, and my hon. friend knows when that investigation took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think I could tell my hon, friend now when it took place, and most assuredly, at that time, the statement as to a former investigation conveyed no specific idea of date to me. Moreover, I might point out to my hon. friend that when he told me that he did not want those charges communicated to the people charged, with a view to their making an answer, but that if I named a commission he would then make his charges, I must confess that I did not charge my mind with the particular words contained in his letter.

I am sure the minister does not *wish to misrepresent the facts, but he is not representing them correctly.
I did not state what he says at the time that conversation took place; I said that as soon as the commission was appointed, then copies of my charges would undoubtedly be sent to the men charged.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, if I am mistaken I want to be corrected, but I think I can turn up the letter the hon. gentleman wrote me making the charges. This is the answer I made to that letter:
I have your letter of the 2nd instant, in which you make charges against Deputy Warden O'Leary and Dr. Phelan.
And so forth.
Before appointing a commissioner to make such inquiry, it would appear proper that the accusations should be submitted to the parties accused, for the purpose of eliciting any reply they may desire to make. Before communicating with these gentlemen, I desire to he informed whether you are willing that I should transmit them copy of your letter or if- you prefer that the accusations he communicated to them in some other form. I may say that for the purpose of the contemplated investigation, my present intention is to issue a commission under the Inquiries Act, Chapter 104 of the Revised Statutes Jif Canada. '
The reply I got to that was:
In reply to yours of the 4th inst., re O'Leary and Phelan, I quite agree that copies of the accusations should be sent to the accused, hut I am not sure that it would be in the best interests of a fair investigation to do more than that. The Commission of Inquiry which you propose to appoint, will bring out the facts and I am quite willing to go before that commission and restate what I have written to you.
There are other officials of the Portsmouth penitentiary whose conduct should he investigated, and I hope that the commission will be given wide powers.
What I understood him to say was " I am quite willing to go before that commission and re-state the charges.

Did you not say that
the first part of the letter should be sent to the men accused?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I understand ithowever, it is perhaps not very material.
I think it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My attention certainly
was not called to the time at which the charge of perjury was made. Perhaps it was [DOT]my oversight, perhaps sufficient attention was not paid on my part. But I only want to point out that when the commissioners said, as they did say, that they did not think that would be a

fair thing to do, it seems to me they were right in saying that, at all events. I may say, moreover, that an opportunity was given in a general way to the gentleman from whom my hon. friend got a large part of the information on which he has based his charges to make any statements with regard to matters anterior to the five years.
With regard to the charges against Dr. Phelan, it is not necessary that I should go over what the commissioners said. It seemed to me they reached a fair conclusion on that subject. What are the consequences that'ought to be drawn from that conclusion is another matter. Tfhe first thing that struck me in dealing with this commission and their report was that the great material thing was to improve the conditions that were complained of.

What conclusion did
they reach about Dr. Phelan?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I thought the hon. gentleman read it himself. However, I will read it if he desires. Here is where they state the responsibility for certain conditions:
It being generally agreed that the condition o: the insane is and has been for years altogether unsatisfactory, the question " who are responsible?" demands an answer. The responsibility falls primarily upon two men, the surgeon and the inspector. The former, in his annual reports, should have given expression to views such as he presented in his evidence before the commission. This was clearly his duty and would have relieved him of responsibility,, but unfortunately a perusal of his reports leaves one with the impression that the state of the insane left nothing to be desired.
Then they go on to deal with Inspector Stewart.
Now here are the particular charges that my hon. friend desires that I shall read. I thought the hon. member was perfectly familiar with them at all events. There were four particular charges made. First he was charged:
(a) With gross political partisanship.
And the commission says:
The counsel for the Government properly says: "I do not propose to- argue that the evidence adduced supports the charge of political partisanship."
The second charge is:
Charge (b). The charge of "using violent and indecent language to a guard in the presence of others."
With regard to this the commission says:
The charge of "using violent and indecent language to a guard in the presence of others " is 
established, but it is claimed that it was used in jest; the evidence leaves this uncertain. In any case, the surgeon entirely forgot the dignity of his position and the discipline of the prison in making use of the language in question ; and the incident discloses an unhealthy state of things.
Then:
(c) With conniving at the absence of a guard at an election trial where said gufird was wanted as a material witness.
With regard to that the commission says:
The commission did not consider this charge to be within the limits of their commission. It occurred thirteen years ago. Some of the parties are dead. It has no bearing on the present state of - the prison.
Then there is the grafting charge, in regard to which they say:
Dr. Phelan admits that in four cases he asked and received a small fee from an applicant for a guard's position as to his physical fitness, and this is a contravention of the statute, as he is not to practise his profession. He says he has not done so for several years. The amount wrongfully taken by him was $4.
The foregoing are the only charges made against Dr. Phelan by Dt Edwards.
I have not been able to find in my examination of the evidence any reason to question the conclusions reached by the commission not only upon these particular charges but in regard to Dr. Phelan by reason of the general conditions in connection with the hospital. The action that ought to be taken in consequence of that is another question. The first thing that seemed important for us to do was to proceed to remedy the conditions. The great condition that called for a remedy in my mind was that in regard to insane patients.

Mr. Chairman, you were particular to call me to order. I would now call your attention to the fact that I do not think there is any quorum and you cannot conduct the proceedings of the committee without a quorum.

The hon. gentleman is
mistaken.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is probably my duty
to make the count. There are 22 members

in the House, which is two more than a quorum.
The House haying resumed in Committee of Supply, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The first thing that seemed to call for improvement was the condition in regard to the insane convicts. Sometimes, when you improve a system, you alter the situation in regard to individuals. Very shortly after the close of last session I took up the matter of the removal of the insane. It was not a thing that could be done in a day. Arms were not held wide open to take these people off our hands. It was a matter of persuading the provincial authorities to allow these men to be removed. It took some months of correspondence, and it might have been done more promptly if there had not been other matters of considerable importance that occupied a great deal of the time of the Minister of Justice. We have not lived an ordinary year, and it is not only penitentiary matters that have had to wait. It was necessary for me to deal with this matter personally before I could bring about any consent to take these insane persons off our hands. I do not think this is the best -way to deal with this question. I hope we shall have an institution under Dominion control for convicts of this class, but in the meantime we have adopted the best possible method of disposing of the matter. We are now dealing with the whole system of the regulations and with the whole body of the recommendations. They are important recommendations. Many of them commend themselves to my judgment, although I do not agree with them all. I have taken means of ascertaining to what extent precisely they ought to be carried out. I thought that in dealing with them it was a reasonable and fair thing that I should endeavour to have the views of the men who have experience in administering the penitentiaries. I do not look upon them as being infallible, but I think it is the part of wisdom to have the benefit of their judgment. These recommendations have been submitted to all the different wardens and we have received the last of their reports. We propose now to take up the question of making regulations.
As regards what has been said about tubbing and hosing, it is hardly fair, although I do not impute any intention of unfairness, to let it go broadcast to the world that this tubbing is a matter of recent
occurrence. I followed the hon. gentleman as carefully as I could, and if I am not mistaken the last case which he described as tubbing was a case that occurred seven years before the evidence was given. At all events, I think we can agree that it was a number of years anterior to the time when the evidence was given, which was in 1913.
I would say that it was five or six years before the evidence was given, which would place it in 1907 or 1908. In face of that circumstance I think we might fairly say that tubbing is not one of the things we have had to contend with to-day. In regard to this punishment of hosing, we have had no recent case. The hon. gentleman says that my answer gave it as May, 1913, and that the witness to whom he referred said it was in July. I think the witness he refers to must be mistaken. It is only a matter of two months anyway, but the reason I think is, as I say, that since the beginning of the wardenship of Colonel Irvine there has been no hosing, and the wardenship of Colonel Irvine began about July. However, it is not very material, except as a matter of absolute accuracy.	,
I think that if my hon. friend looks at his brief he will see that the evidence of Grey is that the last tubbing took place in July, 1913.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am only pointing out why he must have been mistaken, but at all events it does not matter very materially. I wish to say with regard to this punishment that I am not here to defend it. It is a punishment provided under regulations, and I am informed it was approved by Order in Council on the recommendation of the Hon. David Mills, who certainly was known in days past as a most humane man, and I am informed, with the approval of Sir Oliver Mowat, who was also a humane man. I may also point out that the majority of the wardens of the penitentiaries, men of high character, and some of long experience, looked upon this as a desirable form of punishment as a last resort. I do not point this out for the purpose of saying that it is a thing that ought to be continued^ but for the sake of showing that it is not fair to condemn as cruel for the infliction of this punishment a man holding office in which it is prescribed to him by higher authority that this was a suitable punishment to inflect.
We have taken up this whole subject very seriously. We have not been able

to deal with it as promptly as we would in another year, and under other conditions, but it is not helpful to us, when we are trying to introduce improvements, to have it stated in the press and elsewhere that to-day we are doing barbarous things. I heard it stated this afternoon, by an hon. member, that he had seen instruments of torture in the penitentiary, and I would be glad to know what these instruments of torture are, because I certainly have no desire to see them the-e. I want to point out how unfortunate it is that we should have statements go forward, without evidence to support them, as regards the condition of the penitentiaries to-day. I had occasion the other evening to read a statement from the warden of the Kingston penitentiary as to the conditions there to-day, and since he has been warden, and certainly that statement discloses no condition that would justify the description which was given by the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) to-night. I know that the representation made by the hon. gentleman was made in good faith, but fortunately it is without foundation as regards existing conditions in the peniten tiary.
We have completed the arrangements with regard to the care of the insane, and this great improvement necessarily creates a new situation in Kingston penitentiary. There is another question very close to that and which to my mind comes next to it, and that is the question of the whole system of medical attendance. I am sure the hon. member will agree with me that this iis .a most important question. There is more in that question than the position of one man; there is the question whether a different system in securing medical attendance for the convicts is not desirable. Before we come to deal with one isolated case it would be wise for us to come to a conclusion on the subject, because what may happen in a particular case may be affected very gravely by what conclusion may be reached on the general question.
I would ask nothing better than to have the time and the opportunity to bring about improvements in the conditions in our penitentiaries, but I want to say perfectly frankly that I can hold out no hope to anybody who thinks that between now and to-morrow, or between now and next week, or between now and next month, we can have an ideal system of penitentiary administration. It is not possible to effect improvement in such great haste as some people would seem to think. We are at

the beginning of things in the way of improvement, and we will have to go step by step. I believe we will in time bring about improvement, and I hope to have the cooperation of those hon. gentlemen who desire it as earnestly as I do. I shall count upon the assistance of the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), just as I shall count upon the assistance of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), and even upon the assistance of the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike), if he gets himself into a frame of mind where he can believe that my heart is not so full of the spirit of vengeance as he affected to think it was. I do not promise the hon. member that the penitentiaries shall become such pleasure resorts as the Colorado prison that he has described. With the time that has been at my disposal I have done my utmost to bring about improvement, and 1 hope to be able to bring about still greater improvement. It is only frank and honest on my part to say that I believe that those are mistaken who nurse the idea that you can carry on institutions which only have the right to exist because it is the duty of society to punish offenders, by leaving out the element of punishment. I do not pledge myself to any undertaking of that kind. Of more importance than the condition of a particular convict is the question why society has the right to punish a man, and my belief is that the real reason why we have the right to arrest and detain a man is in order that tire punishment he receives may serve as a deterrent to others. Incidental to that punishment I would be glad to do everything I can to reform. Under no circumstances would I countenance anything that would not be humane. But when it is suggested that a penitentiary should cease to be a place where people are punished, that the conditions in it shall be made such as it shall cease to be a punitive institution, then I think the time will have arrived when the state would have no right to maintain such an institution. We have no right, in my judgment, to imprison a man exclusively for the sake of reforming him; our right rests on the necessity of punishing him to protect society, and when the necessity for punishment will have disappeared, the right to imprison will have disappeared also.

Would the hon.
gentleman not go a little further and say

that the punishment should be also with a view to reforming the prisoner?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have said that, so far as incidentally to this punishment you can do reformatory work, my heart is entirely with the hon. member for St. Lawrence. We must all bear in mind, however, not to lose our balance. It may be creditable to our hearts when we lose our balance; but it is incumbent upon some one to keep his head in this regard, and the man who has charge of the administration of justice has to remember that justice requires punishment for violation of law, and punishment such as will operate to deter those who witness it from following the example of the offender. I do not undertake to forget that; I would be forgetting my duty if I did; but
so far as is consistent with that, anything that can be done to help reform the prisoner should be done; and, whether consistent or not with that, we must, of course, be humane. Punishment does not exclude reform. So far as anything is done that ought to be done as punishment, we ought to be assured that our punishment shall be humane; and so far as it is possible to make it serve as a reformatory influence, I shall be glad to co-operate with all those who will co-operate with me, and glad to do my best alone. If I do not get the co-operation which, after what I have heard this evening, I think I have a right to count upon.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 12.05 a.m., Wednesday.
